overview:
This survey maps the literature on adaptive / early-exit computation in large language models and its intersection with demographic fairness, motivated by the research question: does adaptive (depth-budgeted) LLM inference allocate unequal computation and quality to different demographic groups? I first identified 11 authoritative surveys and reviews (well above the 3-5 minimum) that form the cluster skeleton. These span four broad areas: (i) early-exit and adaptive inference (Early-Exit DNNs in NLP; Adaptive Inference through Early-Exit Networks; Split Computing & Early Exiting), (ii) LLM efficiency and inference acceleration (Efficient LLM Inference Serving; Generative LLM Serving; Speculative Decoding), (iii) fairness and bias in LLMs and in ML more broadly (Fairness in LLMs; Bias & Fairness in LLMs; LLM Fairness Taxonomy; Bias & Fairness in ML), and (iv) confidence calibration (Calibration in Deep Learning). I then assembled 71 real, deduplicated primary papers into 7 thematic clusters: Early-Exit & Adaptive-Depth Computation; Speculative & Self-Speculative Decoding; LLM Inference Acceleration (quantization/pruning/KV-cache/attention); Demographic Fairness & Bias in LLMs; Fairness of Model Compression; Confidence Calibration & Uncertainty; and Layer-wise Representation Maturity & Interpretability.

The single most important observation is that the DIRECT intersection of this work — demographic fairness of early-exit computation- and quality-allocation — has essentially no dedicated prior literature. The closest published analogues are (a) the fairness of model compression (pruning/quantization/distillation), which establishes that an efficiency transform preserving average accuracy can still redistribute error onto minority groups, and (b) group-disparity evaluation in LLM generation. This confirms the novelty of the proposed 'computational allocation fairness' perspective: the research must bridge the adaptive-compute machinery (confidence/entropy/learned routers, self-speculative drafts, exit-depth distributions) with the fairness vocabulary (parity, counterfactual invariance, accuracy/quality gaps, group-level calibration), which currently live in largely separate literatures. Because calibration (ECE, temperature scaling, selective prediction) is the exit criterion in most early-exit methods, and because layer-wise probing shows that demographic-attribute representations 'mature' at different depths, both are core mechanistic levers for the proposed fairness decomposition (Fairness Gap ≈ Exit-Distribution Disparity + Layer-wise Capability Disparity). Cross-cutting open questions and recommended directions are flagged in each cluster and survey.

surveys.title: A Survey of Early Exit Deep Neural Networks in NLP
surveys.scope: Reviews early-exit methods for NLP models (encoder and decoder), including exit criteria (confidence, entropy, patience, hash), multi-exit architectures, training schemes (self-distillation, layer dropout), and efficiency/quality trade-offs, with a focus on NLP tasks and emerging LLM settings.
surveys.taxonomy: Exit architectures (branch/multi-exit); exit criteria (confidence, entropy, margin, patience, learned router); training (self-distillation, layer dropout, logit matching); efficiency metrics (FLOPs/latency); evaluation (accuracy vs compute).
surveys.openQuestions: How do exit criteria behave under distribution shift and across demographic groups? Are per-exit heads calibrated? How to design exits that preserve group-equal quality?
surveys.recommendedDirections: Group-aware exit thresholds; fairness-regularized training of exit heads; per-group risk control; benchmarking exit-depth distributions across protected attributes.

surveys.title: Adaptive Inference through Early-Exit Networks: Design, Challenges and Directions
surveys.scope: Foundational survey of early-exit (adaptive inference) networks: where exits are placed, how the decision to exit is made, how accuracy and latency trade off, and the open design challenges and research directions.
surveys.taxonomy: Exit placement; gating/decision mechanisms; training strategies; latency-accuracy trade-off; application domains.
surveys.openQuestions: What is the right place to put exits? Are early-exit decisions reliable under uncertainty? Do they allocate compute fairly across examples?
surveys.recommendedDirections: Learned exit policies; calibration-aware gating; robustness and fairness of exit decisions; system-level integration.

surveys.title: Split Computing and Early Exiting for Deep Learning Applications: Survey and Research Challenges
surveys.scope: Surveys split-computing (deploying neural networks across edge/cloud) and early-exit techniques together, covering when/where computation is offloaded or halted to reduce latency/resource use, and the open research challenges.
surveys.taxonomy: Split computing (model partitioning, layer offloading); early exiting (halt/exit criteria); resource-constrained inference; communication/computation trade-offs.
surveys.openQuestions: How to combine splitting and early exit? Does compute allocation depend on input content in ways that affect different user groups unequally?
surveys.recommendedDirections: Fair resource allocation at the system level; content-dependent compute augmentation; latency fairness across users.

surveys.title: Taming the Titans: A Survey of Efficient LLM Inference Serving
surveys.scope: Survey of efficient LLM inference serving, covering model-level optimizations (speculative decoding, quantization, pruning, dynamic depth) and system-level techniques (batching, KV-cache management, scheduling) for throughput/latency/cost.
surveys.taxonomy: Model-level speedups (speculative decoding, quantization, sparsity, early exit); system-level serving (batching, caching, scheduling, memory management); latency/throughput/cost trade-offs.
surveys.openQuestions: How do serving-stage optimizations interact with output quality? Are compute/latency savings distributed equally among requests or users?
surveys.recommendedDirections: Fair scheduling; audit of per-request compute allocation; combining model- and system-level efficiency with fairness constraints.

surveys.title: Towards Efficient Generative Large Language Model Serving: A Survey from Algorithms to Systems
surveys.scope: Comprehensive survey of generative LLM serving covering both algorithmic acceleration (speculative decoding, quantization, pruning, distillation) and systems (scheduling, batching, caching), and how they combine to reduce end-to-end inference cost.
surveys.taxonomy: Algorithmic acceleration (draft-verify, model compression, early exit); systems optimization (batching, KV cache, scheduling, memory); end-to-end serving pipelines.
surveys.openQuestions: What are the quality and equity costs of algorithmic acceleration at serving scale? How to measure compute fairness in a serving stack?
surveys.recommendedDirections: Per-request latency/cost attribution; fairness-aware scheduling; integrating early-exit policies with serving systems.

surveys.title: Speculative Decoding and Beyond: An In-Depth Survey of Techniques
surveys.scope: Deep survey of speculative decoding techniques (external draft models, self-speculative decoding, multi-token prediction, acceptance sampling) that accelerate LLM decoding while preserving output quality / distribution.
surveys.taxonomy: Draft-then-verify; external vs self draft (early-exit draft); draft granularity (token vs feature space); acceptance-criteria; lossless vs approximate acceleration.
surveys.openQuestions: Is speculative decoding exactly distribution-preserving, and does its acceptance rate vary across inputs/groups? How do early-exit drafts interact with fairness?
surveys.recommendedDirections: Measure acceptance-rate distributions across demographic groups; design drafts/draft-verification that preserve group-equal quality and compute.

surveys.title: A Survey on Fairness in Large Language Models
surveys.scope: Survey of fairness in LLMs: definitions, sources of bias in data/training/inference, evaluation methods and benchmarks, and mitigation approaches, with attention to generative and downstream-task settings.
surveys.taxonomy: Fairness definitions (group, individual, counterfactual, procedural); bias sources (data, representation, training, decoding); evaluation (metrics, benchmarks); mitigation (pre-, in-, post-processing).
surveys.openQuestions: Which fairness notion best captures LLM harms? How to standardize metrics for generative fairness? Is inference-time behavior a fairness lever?
surveys.recommendedDirections: Group-disparity evaluation of generated outputs; standardized metrics; auditing inference-stage choices (including adaptive computation) for equity.

surveys.title: Bias and Fairness in Large Language Models: A Survey
surveys.scope: A highly cited survey of bias and fairness in LLMs that organizes the field into intrinsic (data/representation), contextual, and extrinsic (downstream-task) bias, cataloguing datasets, metrics, and debiasing methods and critiquing evaluation practice.
surveys.taxonomy: Intrinsic vs contextual vs extrinsic bias; bias sources; evaluation datasets (BBQ, BOLD, StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs); metrics; mitigation methods.
surveys.openQuestions: Are current benchmarks/metrics sufficient and standard? How do metrics conflate different fairness notions? Does bias scale with capability?
surveys.recommendedDirections: Standardized, robust fairness metrics; evaluation across newer models and tasks; stage-by-stage auditing including inference; intersectional and multilingual evaluation.

surveys.title: Fairness in Large Language Models: A Taxonomic Survey
surveys.scope: Taxonomic survey of fairness in LLMs that maps fairness definitions, bias sources, evaluation methods, and mitigation approaches across the LLM life cycle (data, pre-training, fine-tuning, inference).
surveys.taxonomy: Life-cycle stages (data, pre-training, fine-tuning, inference); fairness definitions; evaluation metrics and protocols; mitigation techniques per stage.
surveys.openQuestions: How to evaluate fairness per life-cycle stage? Is inference a first-class stage for fairness? How to transfer classical fairness metrics to generation?
surveys.recommendedDirections: Stage-specific evaluation protocols; treating inference as a fairness-relevant stage; standardizing metrics; auditing adaptive/inference-time behavior.

surveys.title: A Survey on Bias and Fairness in Machine Learning
surveys.scope: Foundational survey of bias and fairness in machine learning: definitions, taxonomies of bias (in data, algorithm, user-interaction), fairness notions and metrics (parity, equalized odds, counterfactual), and mitigation (pre-, in-, post-processing).
surveys.taxonomy: Bias taxonomy (data, algorithmic, interaction); fairness notions (statistical parity, equalized odds, individual, counterfactual); mitigation (pre/in/post-processing); metrics.
surveys.openQuestions: Which fairness metric best matches a given deployment? How do metrics interact? How to audit non-classification (generative) systems?
surveys.recommendedDirections: Metric choice guidance; auditing generative/adaptive systems; connecting bias-in-data to downstream disparity.

surveys.title: Calibration in Deep Learning: A Survey of the State-of-the-Art
surveys.scope: Survey of confidence calibration in deep learning: definitions of calibration (ECE, Brier), causes of miscalibration, post-hoc methods (temperature scaling, Platt, binning), and training-based calibration, with discussion of LLM frontiers.
surveys.taxonomy: Calibration metrics (ECE, Brier, reliability diagrams); post-hoc calibration (temperature scaling, Platt, isotonic/binning); train-time calibration; multi-class/structured calibration; LLM calibration.
surveys.openQuestions: Do confidence scores mean the same thing across groups? How to calibrate when labels are ambiguous? Is calibration the right basis for early-exit decisions?
surveys.recommendedDirections: Group-wise calibration; calibration-aware selective/early-exit decision rules; per-group ECE; measuring confidence reliability by subgroup.

clusters.name: Early-Exit & Adaptive-Depth Computation in LLMs
clusters.summary: The core method cluster: multi-exit transformers that stop computation after a chosen layer per input/example, using confidence, entropy, patience, hash-based, or learned-router exit criteria. This is the mechanism the research examines for unequal compute/quality allocation across demographic groups. Anchored by the early-exit surveys (S1-S3).
openQuestions: Do different demographic groups exit at systematically different depths (exit-distribution disparity)?
Is the confidence/entropy that drives exit equally reliable across groups? (calibration disparity)
Are accuracy-vs-depth curves different across groups, so a fixed threshold yields unequal quality? (layer-wise capability disparity)
Can a learned exit router be trained to be group-fair?

clusters.name: Speculative & Self-Speculative Decoding
clusters.summary: Acceleration via draft-then-verify: an external draft model or an internal early-exit draft proposes tokens the full model verifies. Self-speculative variants (LayerSkip, Draft&Verify, Kangaroo) reuse the model's own early exit as the draft, making the early-exit quality and acceptance rate a direct, measurable driver of both speed and per-input compute. Anchored by S6.
openQuestions: Does the draft acceptance rate (and hence per-token compute saved) differ across demographic groups?
Does lossless verification preserve the exact output distribution for all groups, or only in aggregate?
Can self-speculative drafting be calibrated to be group-fair?

clusters.name: LLM Inference Acceleration: Quantization, Pruning, KV-Cache & Attention
clusters.summary: The efficiency field that early-exit sits within (and is compared against): post-training quantization, structural/unstructured pruning, KV-cache compression, attention kernel / IO optimization, and depth-layer dropping. These provide the baseline transforms and the 'computation budget' framing for auditing equal allocation. Anchored by S4, S5.
openQuestions: Which efficiency transform most changes per-group output quality?
Is dropping layers (a depth-budgeting primitive) fairness-neutral or does it hurt specific groups?
How do KV-cache eviction and quantization interact with adaptive depth fairness?

clusters.name: Demographic Fairness & Bias in LLMs (Definitions, Metrics, Benchmarks)
clusters.summary: The fairness vocabulary and instrumentation the research will reuse: bias benchmarks (BBQ, BOLD, WinoBias, StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs, RealToxicityPrompts), fairness metrics (parity, accuracy gap, bias score, stereotype preference, toxicity), and group-disparity evaluation lenses. Anchored by S7-S10.
openQuestions: Which fairness notion (parity, counterfactual, accuracy gap) best captures adaptive-inference harm?
How to measure per-group accuracy/quality gaps when computation is budgeted?
Do the standard benchmarks have enough coverage to detect early-exit- induced disparity?
How to aggregate accuracy and bias (the 'bias score' tension) in a fair-decision-aware way?

clusters.name: Fairness of Model Compression (Quantization, Pruning, Distillation)
clusters.summary: The closest existing analogue to the proposed research: systems and studies showing that a compression/efficiency transform which preserves average accuracy can still disproportionately degrade underrepresented groups, plus fairness-aware compression objectives. Supplied directly by primary papers (no dedicated survey found; noted).
openQuestions: What is the general mechanism by which compression redistributes error onto minority groups, and does it transfer to depth-budgeted (early-exit) inference?
Can a fairness penalty be added to the compression/exit objective without hurting efficiency?
Is there a principled accuracy/efficiency/fairness trade-off curve, and how should it be exposed?

clusters.name: Confidence Calibration & Uncertainty for LLMs
clusters.summary: Because most early-exit methods use a confidence/entropy threshold as the exit criterion, calibration quality across groups is a primary mechanism for the fairness analysis. Covers calibration metrics (ECE, Brier), post-hoc methods (temperature scaling), LLM-specific confidence elicitation, and semantic/selective uncertainty. Anchored by S11.
openQuestions: Is confidence calibrated differently across demographic groups, so a shared threshold exits at different true-error levels?
How to measure group-wise ECE for exit decisions?
Do selective-prediction / abstention methods perform differently per group?
Can temperature scaling or calibration be applied per-group before exiting?

clusters.name: Layer-wise Representation Maturity & Interpretability
clusters.summary: Provides the mechanism for hypothesis H2 (quality disparity): probing/interpreting how representations evolve across depth, whether demographic attributes become separable at specific depths, and whether layer importance is heterogeneous. Directly supports 'representation maturity' as the quantity to compare across groups. Anchor supplied by primary probing papers.
openQuestions: Do demographic attributes (gender, race, etc.) become linearly separable at different depths for different groups?
Is layer importance/contribution heterogeneous such that a fixed exit depth preserves different information for different groups?
How to operationalize 'representation maturity' (linear-separable / probe accuracy) as a per-group, per-layer metric?

papers.title: BERT Loses Patience: Fast and Robust Inference with Early Exit (PABEE)
papers.abstract: Adds inexpensive classification exits to every layer of BERT and stops inference early via a patience rule (k consecutive agreeing predictions), so easy inputs exit early and hard ones run deeper, cutting compute with little accuracy loss.
papers.oneLiner: Patience-based early exit for encoder transformers that waits for k agreeing predictions before stopping.
papers.keyFinding: Patience-based exits remain robust to noisy intermediate predictions, saving significant FLOPs with minimal accuracy loss and beating confidence-only early exits.
papers.weakness: Encoder-only and classification-centric; not designed for decoder-only, long-context generative LLMs or token-level decoding.
papers.implication: The exit decision is input-dependent, so per-input compute is unequal (a seed of the fairness concern).
papers.contributions: Multi-exit BERT with per-layer classifiers; patience-based stopping rule; large FLOPs savings with minor accuracy loss on GLUE.
papers.methods: Multi-exit BERT, per-layer classifiers, patience-based voting/stopping, single forward pass.
papers.experiments: GLUE classification with BERT-base/large; accuracy vs speed curves.
papers.results: Up to ~6-9x speedup at negligible accuracy loss in some configs.
papers.limitations: Classification-centric; no generation or KV-cache/batching; global threshold/patience tuned on aggregate accuracy.
papers.futureDirections: Extend patience exits to decoder LLMs, token-level rationales, and sequence-level cost control.
papers.insights: Sample-dependent compute means inference cost is a function of the input, not a constant.
papers.relevance: Establishes the foundational input-conditional-compute mechanism that can allocate fewer layers to 'easy' (possibly group-skewed) inputs.

papers.title: DeeBERT: Dynamic Early Exiting for Accelerating BERT Inference
papers.abstract: Inserts lightweight classifiers into intermediate BERT layers and exits per sample when confidence exceeds a threshold, accelerating inference while largely preserving accuracy.
papers.oneLiner: Confidence-threshold early exit via intermediate output heads.
papers.keyFinding: Early exits cut computation substantially with a small accuracy drop, but only after fine-tuning the internal classifiers and tuning a global threshold.
papers.weakness: Requires fine-tuning (not plug-in); hard global threshold; classification only.
papers.implication: The threshold that decides compute spend is tuned globally on aggregate accuracy, so any group with lower confidence is handled differently.
papers.contributions: Multi-exit BERT with intermediate classifiers; thresholded early-exit formulation; accuracy/latency baseline metrics.
papers.methods: Transformer with intermediate classification heads, entropy/softmax confidence threshold, task fine-tuning.
papers.experiments: GLUE-style classification with BERT-base; accuracy & speedup.
papers.results: ~2-4x speedup on some tasks at minimal accuracy loss.
papers.limitations: Threshold tuned on validation set; not distribution-adaptive; global criterion.
papers.futureDirections: Per-group exits; calibration-aware confidence to make exits more equitable.
papers.insights: A single global confidence threshold is a blunt instrument that silently spends different compute per input.
papers.relevance: Illustrates that the threshold deciding compute spend is global, so systematically lower-confidence inputs get more compute (or are cut off and misclassified).

papers.title: FastBERT: A Self-distilling BERT with Adaptive Inference Time
papers.abstract: Adds classifier branches at each layer and lets each sample stop at a different depth, with self-distillation so intermediate representations are supervised toward the final output.
papers.oneLiner: Sample-adaptive inference where each layer has a classifier branch and samples exit at different depths.
papers.keyFinding: Self-distillation makes intermediate predictions informative enough for early exits to mirror final-layer behavior, enabling large speedups with minimal loss.
papers.weakness: Encoder-only/classification; branch confidence can be mis-calibrated; no generation.
papers.implication: Because compute is input-dependent and driven by self-distilled confidence, any confidence bias transfers into compute-allocation bias.
papers.contributions: Multi-branch transformer with per-layer classifiers; self-distillation of intermediate layers; speed/accuracy frontier.
papers.methods: Multi-layer classifier branches, self-distillation (logit matching), adaptive exit on sample confidence.
papers.experiments: GLUE classification with BERT-base; accuracy vs latency/FLOPs.
papers.results: Several-times speedup with small accuracy degradation.
papers.limitations: Needs substantial fine-tuning/distillation; static confidence threshold; no token-level depth control.
papers.futureDirections: Extend self-distilled adaptive exits to decoders and per-token depth; study confidence-bias transfer.
papers.insights: The model's own confidence routes compute, so the method inherits the model's confidence bias.
papers.relevance: Shows adaptive compute is driven by self-distilled confidence, so biased confidence across groups directly biases compute allocation.

papers.title: Confident Adaptive Language Modeling (CALM)
papers.abstract: For decoder-only next-token LMs, CALM dynamically chooses how many layers to run per token based on softmax confidence, with a risk-controlling formulation bounding the probability of premature stopping.
papers.oneLiner: Per-token adaptive depth for generative LLMs, exiting when the current layer's softmax confidence is high enough.
papers.keyFinding: CALM terminates most tokens after a few layers while matching full-depth quality, using a risk-controlling threshold with statistical guarantees.
papers.weakness: Threshold tuning on English corpora; per-token exits complicate KV-cache and batch GPU utilization; no group-wise analysis.
papers.implication: Every token's compute depends on the model's self-reported confidence, directly redistributing work per token.
papers.contributions: Per-token early exit for decoder-only LMs; risk-controlling threshold; multiple exit heads; large FLOPs reductions.
papers.methods: Multi-exit decoder-only LM, softmax-confidence stopping rule, risk-controlling prediction threshold, training of exit heads.
papers.experiments: Text generation (e.g., WikiText-103) and LM benchmarks; quality vs compute.
papers.results: High-quality generation at a fraction of compute; most tokens exit after a few layers.
papers.limitations: Risk control is on aggregate loss, not per-group loss; single probability-vector confidence; no fairness/subgroup analysis.
papers.futureDirections: Per-group risk control; group-calibrated confidence; KV-cache-friendly exits.
papers.insights: The stopping criterion is the model's own confidence, making compute allocation a learned, input-dependent decision that can skew demographically.
papers.relevance: The canonical LLM early-exit method; its per-token confidence-driven depth allocation is exactly the mechanism that could deliver unequal compute to groups.

papers.title: A Simple Hash-Based Early Exiting Approach For Language Understanding and Generation
papers.abstract: Uses a cheap hash function over token embeddings to decide early exit for each token, making early exiting nearly free and applicable to both understanding and generation.
papers.oneLiner: A training-free, hash-based early-exit controller keyed on the token itself rather than learned confidence.
papers.keyFinding: A simple token hash is surprisingly competitive, showing much of the speedup comes from skipping layers on predictable tokens rather than sophisticated confidence estimators.
papers.weakness: Coarse, uncertainty-agnostic signal; brittle across domains; no subgroup evaluation.
papers.implication: The exit signal being a function of token identity means compute allocation is purely a function of surface token, independent of model confidence.
papers.contributions: Lightweight training-free hash-based early-exit controller; applies to understanding and generation; quality-preserving compute reduction.
papers.methods: Deterministic hash over token embeddings/positions to pick exit layer, with existing encoders/decoders.
papers.experiments: GLUE-style understanding and text summarization; accuracy and latency.
papers.results: Competitive speedups with minimal quality degradation, comparable to learned confidence exits in some settings.
papers.limitations: Not uncertainty-aware; token-hash design may be fragile; no subgroup analysis.
papers.futureDirections: Learn hash/routing conditioned on group/surprise; combine hash cheapness with calibration.
papers.insights: Any input-dependent exit policy (learned or fixed) can produce unequal compute across groups.
papers.relevance: Shows the exit decision need not rely on model confidence, sharpening the point that any input-dependent policy can yield unequal group compute.

papers.title: SkipDecode: Autoregressive Skip Decoding with Batching and Caching for Efficient LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Builds a per-layer skip decision during autoregressive decoding while remaining compatible with KV-cache batching, making layer skipping practical in batched LLM serving.
papers.oneLiner: A system-oriented early-exit method that makes layer skipping practical in batched, KV-cached LLM inference.
papers.keyFinding: Layer skipping can be made batching- and caching-friendly, unlocking real wall-clock decode speedups in a serving stack, not just FLOPs savings.
papers.weakness: Heuristic/confidence per-token skip decisions; quality can degrade on hard tokens; gains depend on batch composition.
papers.implication: In batched serving, per-token skip decisions determine per-token GPU work, and batch composition shapes achievable speedup.
papers.contributions: Layer-wise skip-decoding compatible with KV caching; serving-path integration; wall-clock acceleration.
papers.methods: Per-layer confidence/volatility skip decisions, KV-cache-compatible forward subsets, batch-aware scheduling.
papers.experiments: Decoder-only LLM decoding workloads; end-to-end latency and quality (perplexity).
papers.results: Reduces decode latency with small quality cost, notably in throughput terms.
papers.limitations: Quality loss under aggressive skipping; token-local heuristics; no group/fairness analysis.
papers.futureDirections: Learn principled skip policies; measure skip decisions across input/group types.
papers.insights: System-level batching makes 'compute per token' a first-class measurable quantity.
papers.relevance: Bridges early-exit research to serving practice, showing how compute is reallocated per token in batched decode where fairness of allocation matters.

papers.title: Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically allocating compute in transformer-based language models
papers.abstract: Routes each token through a variable number of transformer blocks via a learned top-k selection of which tokens occupy a block at each layer, allocating compute dynamically during training and inference.
papers.oneLiner: A routing-based scheme where each layer processes only a top-k subset of tokens, dynamically allocating compute per token.
papers.keyFinding: Models can learn which tokens deserve more compute; capacity-based MoD matches or beats dense quality while using much fewer FLOPs per token.
papers.weakness: Routing is by capacity/FLOPs not correctness on hard samples; optimizer-sensitive; not a decode-time confidence exit.
papers.implication: Token-level routing is learned, so which tokens receive more compute is an emergent, trainable property, potentially correlated with token frequency/domain.
papers.contributions: Capacity-based dynamic compute at block level (MoD); learns to allocate more compute to harder tokens; matches dense quality with lower FLOPs.
papers.methods: Learned top-k token routing per block, capacity allocation, trained end-to-end with the language model.
papers.experiments: Language modeling pretraining at multiple scales; quality vs FLOP-efficiency.
papers.results: Comparable quality at roughly 50% FLOPs, with latency of a smaller model.
papers.limitations: Static per-forward capacity routing; no per-token confidence; routing not analyzed for equity.
papers.futureDirections: Study whether learned routing favors certain token/domain types; add fairness constraints to routing.
papers.insights: Dynamic compute can be learned, not just thresholded, so compute allocation across inputs is an optimization outcome.
papers.relevance: Key alternative to confidence exits: a learned router allocates compute per token, raising the same fairness-of-allocation question.

papers.title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
papers.abstract: Introduces gated recursion depth where each token can recurse within a transformer block a variable number of times, giving token-wise adaptive depth and computation at inference.
papers.oneLiner: A token-level adaptive-depth architecture where each token recurses a learned number of times per layer.
papers.keyFinding: Per-token recursion depth improves the efficiency/quality frontier: harder tokens recurse more, easy tokens less, matching or beating dense baselines with less compute.
papers.weakness: Recursion hardware/serving implications non-trivial; learned depth distribution not analyzed for demographic/domain equity.
papers.implication: Depth is a learned per-token variable, so the model decides how much to 'ponder' each input — a direct analogue of unequal compute allocation.
papers.contributions: Mixture-of-recursions with per-token recursive depth; adaptive depth improves compute/quality trade-off; token-wise compute allocation for decoders.
papers.methods: Gated recursive transformer blocks, learned depth/exit gating, language-modeling objective, adaptive token-level computation.
papers.experiments: Language modeling and downstream generation; loss vs compute and depth distribution.
papers.results: Better efficiency/quality Pareto front; token-level depth varies with input difficulty.
papers.limitations: Complex gating/recursion; no subgroup compute-equity analysis.
papers.futureDirections: Characterize per-token depth distribution across domains/demographics; constrain depth to be group-fair.
papers.insights: The model learns to 'think longer' on some tokens; the question is whether it systematically thinks longer/shorter for particular groups.
papers.relevance: A modern token-level adaptive-compute architecture whose learned depth distribution is precisely what a fairness analysis should measure.

papers.title: Dynamic layer selection in decoder-only transformers
papers.abstract: Trains a routing mechanism that selects a variable subset of decoder-only transformer layers to run per input, so different inputs use different effective depths.
papers.oneLiner: Learned per-input routing over decoder layers, activating a different subset per sample.
papers.keyFinding: A small learned router can predict which layers an input needs without retraining the backbone, yielding compute savings with limited quality loss.
papers.weakness: Router trained per task/domain; coarse layer selection; no subpopulation analysis.
papers.implication: Which layers run is a learned function of the input, making compute budget a learned, input-dependent quantity.
papers.contributions: Learned layer-selection router for decoder-only transformers; plug-in routing over frozen backbones; reduced FLOPs.
papers.methods: Learned routing head over layer subsets, network-rewiring/selection, applied to frozen decoder-only models at inference.
papers.experiments: Decoder-only transformer tasks (generation/LM); accuracy vs compute for routed vs full-depth inference.
papers.results: Meaningful FLOPs reduction with acceptable accuracy.
papers.limitations: Task/domain-specific; needs training data per setting; no fairness/subgroup calibration.
papers.futureDirections: Train routers with fairness constraints; audit routing decisions across demographic groups.
papers.insights: Router-based layer selection makes the compute-allocation decision explicit and trainable — the cleanest setting to inject or audit fairness.
papers.relevance: Demonstrates a learned exit/router policy for LLMs whose input-dependent decisions are exactly what would need fairness auditing.

papers.title: Depth-Adaptive Transformer
papers.abstract: Proposes depth-adaptive computation in Transformers, letting each input decide how many layers to use (early exit) to reduce computation while preserving quality.
papers.oneLiner: Per-example depth-adaptive inference: each input exits at its own best depth.
papers.keyFinding: Combining per-example halting/classifiers with layer-specific classifiers lets models stop early on easy inputs while preserving quality on hard ones.
papers.weakness: Efficiency-focused; fairness across groups not analyzed.
papers.implication: Because exit depth is chosen per example, if accuracy-vs-depth curves differ across groups, exiting is not fairness-neutral.
papers.contributions: Depth-adaptive inference algorithms (halt/skip) for Transformers trading computation for quality.
papers.methods: Halting mechanisms/classifiers at intermediate layers (confidence- or prior-layer-based) to decide whether to stop.
papers.experiments: Machine translation and language modeling; quality vs FLOPs.
papers.results: Substantial compute savings (often 2-3x) with little quality loss; easy examples exit early.
papers.limitations: No fairness/subgroup analysis; halting heuristics; sequential-decoding interactions.
papers.futureDirections: Analyze per-group exit decisions and accuracy; add fairness constraints to routing.
papers.insights: Real early-exit systems choose depth per input, so group-varying accuracy-vs-depth curves are a fairness risk.
papers.relevance: Establishes depth-adaptive inference as an efficiency method whose per-input depth choice can amplify group differences if maturity differs by group.

papers.title: The Right Tool for the Job: Matching Model and Instance Complexities
papers.abstract: Shows that NLP models can adapt computation to input complexity, routing easier instances to smaller models and harder ones to deeper models.
papers.oneLiner: Different examples need different compute, so adaptive depth beats one fixed model.
papers.keyFinding: A complexity estimator/router sends light outputs for easy instances and deep computation for hard ones, improving the efficiency-accuracy frontier.
papers.weakness: No demographic-fairness analysis; relies on complexity measures that may correlate with group.
papers.implication: If complexity (and hence chosen depth) correlates with a demographic group, early-exit routing produces group-skewed accuracy.
papers.contributions: Model-routing framework matching capacity to instance complexity; analysis of complexity distributions.
papers.methods: Complexity estimator/router allocating compute per example across a set of models or depths.
papers.experiments: Multiple NLP tasks with complexity measures and accuracy/compute trade-offs.
papers.results: Routing by complexity gives better efficiency/accuracy than a single model; instances need different depths.
papers.limitations: Fairness not analyzed; routing based on difficulty not group; may entrench bias.
papers.futureDirections: Audit routed depth by demographic group; enforce fair-routing constraints.
papers.insights: Depth allocation is instance-driven, so if complexity is group-correlated, fairness gaps emerge.
papers.relevance: Demonstrates early-exit depth is chosen per instance, so group differences in maturity yield unequal accuracy.

papers.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Introduces speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes tokens that a larger target model verifies in parallel, giving 2-3x wall-clock speedups while provably preserving the exact output distribution.
papers.oneLiner: Use a small draft model to guess tokens, then verify them in parallel with the big model for exact-distribution speedups.
papers.keyFinding: Speculative decoding achieves 2-3x faster decoding while provably producing the identical output distribution as the target model.
papers.weakness: Requires a matching draft model plus extra memory; speedup collapses when draft and target distributions diverge.
papers.implication: Because sampling quality is preserved exactly, this form of acceleration does not itself alter model behavior.
papers.contributions: Verification-based speculative decoding framework with theoretically exact token sampling.
papers.methods: Draft proposes tokens; target verifies in parallel; token-level rejection sampling preserves the target distribution.
papers.experiments: T5-XXL and GPT-2-class models vs baseline autoregressive; latency and output quality.
papers.results: 2-3x speedup with no measurable output-quality degradation.
papers.limitations: Two-model memory cost; gain depends on draft-target alignment; low-batch autoregressive focus.
papers.futureDirections: Learned draft models, larger batches, other generation tasks.
papers.insights: Acceleration can be lossless if the same distribution is sampled, contrasting with approximate early-exit methods.
papers.relevance: Demonstrates lossless acceleration; early-exit fairness work must justify why its quality/fairness trade-offs are acceptable when lossless options exist.

papers.title: Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads
papers.abstract: Adds multiple parallel decoding heads on top of a frozen base LLM to predict several future tokens at once, combined with tree-based attention and typical-acceptance sampling, with no separate draft model.
papers.oneLiner: Add parallel prediction heads to the base model so several tokens are guessed and verified in one step.
papers.keyFinding: Medusa delivers ~2.2x decoding speedup on Vicuna-7B/33B and 2.3x on MT-Bench while preserving quality, with no extra draft model.
papers.weakness: Requires training/alignment of heads; speedup bounded by acceptance rates.
papers.implication: A model can predict its own future tokens with auxiliary heads, avoiding the extra-draft-model cost.
papers.contributions: Multiple prediction heads; tree-based attention; typical-acceptance sampling to correct rejection bias.
papers.methods: Train parallel Medusa heads on a frozen backbone with an auxiliary loss; tree attention and typical acceptance during decoding.
papers.experiments: Vicuna-7B/13B/33B on MT-Bench and GSM8K vs speculative/self-speculative baselines.
papers.results: 2.2-2.3x speedup with quality matching the baseline.
papers.limitations: Needs training and head memory; typical-acceptance robustness not uniform.
papers.futureDirections: More heads, serving integration, other model families.
papers.insights: A guided multi-token predictor trained on the same model can beat generic external draft models.
papers.relevance: Shows a model-specific accelerator can change token distributions; such output shifts need auditing across demographic groups.

papers.title: EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty
papers.abstract: EAGLE drafts autoregressively in the feature (hidden-state) space rather than token space, conditioning on the target model's feature distribution to lower uncertainty and raise acceptance, achieving 2-3x and up to 5x latency reduction.
papers.oneLiner: Draft in the hidden-feature space instead of token space to make draft predictions far more accurate.
papers.keyFinding: Feature-level drafting sharply raises acceptance rates, giving ~2-3x latency reduction (up to 5x in some settings) while strictly preserving the output distribution.
papers.weakness: Draft header must be retrained per base model; adds memory/complexity.
papers.implication: The space in which you draft (features vs tokens) is a dominant factor in speculative-decoding efficiency.
papers.contributions: Feature-level autoregressive drafting; two-stage training for the draft header.
papers.methods: Draft header recursively predicts next-token features verified by the target; contrastive/self-distillation training.
papers.experiments: Llama2-7B/13B/70B and Vicuna; speedup and acceptance vs strong baselines.
papers.results: 2-3x average speedup, up to 5x, matching or beating the strongest prior methods.
papers.limitations: Model-specific draft-header training; memory overhead; model-dependent gains.
papers.futureDirections: Adaptive acceptance thresholds; cross-architecture generalization; combine with quantization.
papers.insights: Draft accuracy is the lever for speculative decoding, and feature-space drafting is an effective way to get it.
papers.relevance: Highlights that this acceleration family's ceiling is draft precision, which matters when auditing whether acceleration changes output behavior.

papers.title: LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Trains LLMs with layer dropout plus early-exit loss so they can exit at intermediate layers; at inference these exits either provide direct early-exit output or serve as a draft for self-speculative decoding verified by the full model.
papers.oneLiner: Jointly optimizes LLMs to (1) exit early and (2) feed an early-exit draft to the full model for lossless self-speculative decoding.
papers.keyFinding: Combining layer dropout with early-exit self-distillation lets a single model both accelerate via early exit and accelerate losslessly via self-speculation.
papers.weakness: Requires a customized training recipe; early-exit and draft quality both depend on training; decoder-only; exit adds serving complexity.
papers.implication: The early-exit head is both a quality-critical decision point and the draft source, so its confidence behavior drives both speed and correctness.
papers.contributions: Layer dropout + early-exit loss for multi-exit LLMs; self-speculative decoding within a single model; lossless speedups plus configurable early-exit speedups.
papers.methods: Layer dropout during training, early-exit self-distillation, intermediate exit heads, self-speculative draft-verify decoding.
papers.experiments: LLM pretraining and downstream tasks; latency/throughput and quality for both modes.
papers.results: Significant speedups for early-exit and lossless self-speculative decoding with little/no quality loss.
papers.limitations: Training cost and recipe sensitivity; no group-level or fairness analysis of exit/draft behavior.
papers.futureDirections: Analyze where the model exits across input types; audit whether early-exit quality is uniform across groups.
papers.insights: LayerSkip makes early exit a first-class training objective, so exit behavior (and compute allocation) is directly shaped by training data.
papers.relevance: State-of-the-art early-exit + self-speculative LLM method; ideal target for measuring per-token compute/correctness differences across groups.

papers.title: Draft & Verify: Lossless Large Language Model Acceleration via Self-Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Proposes self-speculative decoding: the same LLM drafts tokens by exiting early from an intermediate layer, then verifies them with its full forward pass, yielding lossless acceleration without a separate draft model.
papers.oneLiner: Lossless self-speculative decoding where an early exit acts as the draft model and the full model verifies.
papers.keyFinding: An early-exit draft from the same model can be verified by the full model to give exact match with baseline output while speeding up decoding.
papers.weakness: Draft quality and speedup depend on early-exit accuracy; draft-verify complicates serving; speedup varies by input; no fairness analysis.
papers.implication: Decode speed and correctness hinge on the early-exit draft, so tokens drafted/accepted differently across groups affect both cost and quality.
papers.contributions: Introduces self-speculative decoding (drafting from an internal early exit); guarantees lossless output; practical speedups without extra draft params.
papers.methods: Early-exit draft token proposal from a mid/low layer; full-model verification with rejection/acceptance.
papers.experiments: LLM decoding on generation benchmarks; tokens/sec and throughput vs baseline (lossless = identical output distribution).
papers.results: Meaningful wall-clock speedups while producing identical outputs to full-depth decoding.
papers.limitations: Lossless, but acceptance rate (and speedup) is input-dependent; needs intermediate-layer access; no subgroup analysis.
papers.futureDirections: Study acceptance-rate differences across inputs/groups; calibrate drafts for fair compute savings.
papers.insights: Because verification is lossless, speedup is purely a function of how often the early-exit draft is accepted — a measurable per-input quantity.
papers.relevance: Gives a clean, quantifiable signal (acceptance rate per input) for detecting unequal compute allocation while keeping outputs correct.

papers.title: Kangaroo: Lossless Self-Speculative Decoding via Double Early Exiting
papers.abstract: Uses a lightweight self-drafting mechanism with two early-exit stages — a cheap draft exit and a verification/proposal stage — to accelerate lossless decoding within a single model.
papers.oneLiner: Double early exiting within one model to draft and verify tokens losslessly for faster decoding.
papers.keyFinding: Combining a cheap early-exit draft with a second, more reliable intermediate verification improves acceptance rate and speedup while keeping output lossless.
papers.weakness: Adds architectural complexity (multiple exits); requires intermediate-state access; no fairness/group analysis of accept rate or latency.
papers.implication: The double-exit design allocates compute across two decision points per token, again making compute a token-level predicted quantity.
papers.contributions: Double-early-exit self-speculative decoding; better draft acceptance and larger lossless speedups than single-exit baselines; preserves output distribution.
papers.methods: Two early exits used for draft and verification; self-speculative draft-verify; intermediate-layer access.
papers.experiments: LLM generation benchmarks; speedup and acceptance rate vs single-draft self-speculative baselines.
papers.results: Higher acceptance rates and larger speedups than comparable single-exit self-speculative methods, with lossless output.
papers.limitations: Extra exits add memory/complexity; speedup depends on acceptance distribution; no subgroup fairness analysis.
papers.futureDirections: Measure acceptance-rate/latency distributions across input types/groups; add fairness-aware exit placement.
papers.insights: Adding more exits gives finer-grained control over compute — and more places where unequal allocation could arise.
papers.relevance: Represents the trend toward increasingly fine-grained, model-internal exit policies, the surface where fairness-of-computation should be audited.

papers.title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers
papers.abstract: GPTQ is a one-shot weight quantization method based on approximate second-order information that compresses LLM weights to 3-4 bits while preserving accuracy.
papers.oneLiner: Compress LLM weights to 3-4 bits with a Hessian-based method that keeps accuracy nearly intact.
papers.keyFinding: GPTQ compresses LLMs to 3-4 bits per weight with only a small perplexity increase, giving 2-3x faster inference.
papers.weakness: Upfront second-order computation is costly; weight-only (activations stay high precision); results depend on calibration data.
papers.implication: Post-training quantization can be near-lossless for LLMs without retraining.
papers.contributions: Layer-wise quantization using approximate second-order information; fast batched inverse-Hessian formulation.
papers.methods: Hessian-based (OBQ-style) layer-wise quantization with batched inverse-Hessian approximation and group-size scaling.
papers.experiments: Quantized OPT and BabelGPT models at 3-4 bits; perplexity and memory vs unquantized baselines.
papers.results: 3-4 bit compression with minimal perplexity change and 2-3x speedup.
papers.limitations: Weight-only; needs calibration data; error depends on calibration quality.
papers.futureDirections: Activation-aware methods, very-low-bit regimes, hardware co-design.
papers.insights: Second-order-aware quantization is highly effective, exploiting model-specific structure for compression.
papers.relevance: Low-bit weight compression interacts with the layers an early-exit system keeps, so per-group accuracy auditing is relevant.

papers.title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration
papers.abstract: AWQ identifies a small set of salient weight channels by observing activation magnitudes rather than weight magnitudes, then protects those channels during quantization.
papers.oneLiner: Guard a few important weight channels, found by activation magnitude, to get high-quality low-bit quantization.
papers.keyFinding: AWQ quantizes to 4-bit with much better accuracy than prior methods and enables on-device Llama serving with 3x+ speedups and large memory savings.
papers.weakness: Requires validation-set activation statistics; saliency is per-model; overhead to find salient channels.
papers.implication: Activation statistics, not raw weight magnitudes, determine which weights need protecting in quantization.
papers.contributions: Activation-aware saliency detection, per-channel scaling, hardware-friendly kernel stack for device-side inference.
papers.methods: Detect salient channels from activation magnitude; scale before quantization; group-wise/per-channel quantization.
papers.experiments: Quantized Llama-family and other LLMs; perplexity, downstream tasks, on-device mobile inference.
papers.results: 4-bit quantization with strong accuracy; 3x-faster, memory-efficient on-device serving.
papers.limitations: Requires calibration activations; degrades at very low bit-widths; saliency detection is heuristic.
papers.futureDirections: Better saliency measures, joint weight-activation quantization, stronger kernels.
papers.insights: Activation-driven protection of salient weights is a central design principle for low-bit LLM quantization.
papers.relevance: Shows quantization choices are activation-driven; analogous activation-based checks matter for fairness auditing of early-exit systems.

papers.title: SparseGPT: Massive Language Models Can Be Accurately Pruned in One-Shot
papers.abstract: SparseGPT prunes massive LLMs to 50-60% sparsity in a single shot using a scalable layer-wise method that reformulates pruning as sparse regression, with almost no accuracy loss and no retraining.
papers.oneLiner: Prune giant LLMs down to half their weights in one shot using a scalable sparse-regression method.
papers.keyFinding: SparseGPT removes 50-60% of weights from models up to 175B in one shot with near-zero accuracy loss, without retraining.
papers.weakness: Mostly unstructured sparsity needing specialized hardware for speed; Hessian cost high; accuracy drops at very high sparsity.
papers.implication: Post-training pruning can yield large weight reduction without retraining, but real speed requires hardware support.
papers.contributions: Scalable one-shot pruning; sparse-regression solver; efficient GPU implementation.
papers.methods: Layer-wise pruning cast as sparse regression with per-layer updated Hessian reconstruction and row-wise selection.
papers.experiments: Pruned OPT models up to 175B to 50-60% sparsity; perplexity and zero-shot accuracy.
papers.results: 50-60% sparsity with minimal perplexity/accuracy loss across LLM scales.
papers.limitations: Unstructured sparsity gives limited real speedup without sparse-aware hardware; needs full model in memory.
papers.futureDirections: Structured sparsity variants, combine with quantization, hardware co-design.
papers.insights: LLMs are highly compressible through pruning, but realized speedups depend on structured or hardware support.
papers.relevance: Pruning changes which weights survive; resulting output differences across demographic groups could be audited for fairness.

papers.title: LLM-Pruner: On the Structural Pruning of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: LLM-Pruner performs structural pruning of LLMs by removing coupled structures (attention heads, FFN channels) selected by gradient-based importance in a task-agnostic way, then lightly fine-tunes to recover performance.
papers.oneLiner: Prune whole structures such as heads and channels using gradient importance, then recover with light fine-tuning.
papers.keyFinding: Structural pruning reduces LLaMA-7B to ~2.7B-equivalent FLOPs with only modest loss in zero-shot accuracy.
papers.weakness: Requires fine-tuning recovery; instruction-following degrades; quality loss not zero.
papers.implication: Real hardware speed/memory gains require structural (not just unstructured) pruning, which costs some accuracy.
papers.contributions: Task-agnostic structural pruning via gradient saliency on coupled structures; light post-pruning tuning recipe.
papers.methods: Gradient-based importance scoring; prune grouped structures (heads, FFN channels); short fine-tuning.
papers.experiments: Pruned LLaMA-7B and Vicuna; zero-shot and instruction tasks; FLOPs and memory.
papers.results: ~2.7B-equivalent FLOPs reduction with slight zero-shot degradation and modest memory savings.
papers.limitations: Needs fine-tuning; sensitive to tuning budget; instruction following degrades.
papers.futureDirections: Better importance metrics, task-specific pruning, combine with quantization.
papers.insights: Structural pruning is the practical path to real speedups but requires recovery training.
papers.relevance: Removing attention heads or depth layers changes which language patterns are preserved, directly relevant to fairness auditing.

papers.title: H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: H2O introduces an attention KV-cache eviction policy that keeps a small set of frequently-attended 'heavy-hitter' tokens plus recent tokens, reducing cache memory by up to 20x and improving throughput while maintaining quality.
papers.oneLiner: Keep only the frequently-attended 'heavy-hitter' tokens plus recent ones to shrink the KV cache dramatically.
papers.keyFinding: H2O cuts KV-cache memory by up to 20x and boosts throughput while keeping or improving generation quality.
papers.weakness: Heuristic importance measure; may drop tokens critical for long-context reasoning, so quality can degrade on some tasks.
papers.implication: Not all past tokens matter equally; attention-based selection can greatly reduce memory without much accuracy loss.
papers.contributions: Attention-guided KV-cache eviction framework; heavy-hitter oracle for dynamic cache allocation.
papers.methods: Track accumulated attention per token; retain top heavy-hitters plus a sliding window; update cache dynamically.
papers.experiments: Multiple LLMs and long-context datasets; memory, throughput, quality.
papers.results: Up to 20x cache reduction with higher throughput, preserving quality.
papers.limitations: Heuristic importance; relies on attention as oracle; risk to long-context accuracy.
papers.futureDirections: Learning-based eviction, stronger importance measures, serving integration.
papers.insights: Attention statistics are a strong prior for which keys matter, central to cache compression.
papers.relevance: KV eviction decides which context is remembered; which tokens get dropped could differ across demographic groups.

papers.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
papers.abstract: StreamingLLM observes that streaming LLMs need 'attention sinks' (a few initial tokens) to stabilize attention, combining them with a rolling window to enable stable inference over millions of tokens with constant memory.
papers.oneLiner: Keep a few initial 'sink' tokens in the KV cache so attention stays stable over millions of generated tokens.
papers.keyFinding: Attention sinks plus a local sliding window let LLMs stream over more than 4M tokens with constant memory and no quality collapse.
papers.weakness: Performance depends on sink curation; limited to very long streaming contexts.
papers.implication: KV-cache memory can be made constant even for unbounded generation by retaining a minimal set of sink tokens.
papers.contributions: Analysis of the attention-sink phenomenon; streaming-inference method with fixed cache and local window.
papers.methods: Keep a few initial sink tokens plus a sliding window of recent tokens, avoiding recomputation of full history.
papers.experiments: Llama-2, MPT, Pythia; streaming tasks and sequences longer than 4M tokens.
papers.results: Stable streaming beyond 4M tokens with constant memory and efficient throughput.
papers.limitations: Sink initialization matters; limited to streaming; quality not uniform across tasks.
papers.futureDirections: Better sink selection, combine with cache compression, training-aware sink design.
papers.insights: Attention needs a small persistent anchor set, a subtle cue for cache-management design.
papers.relevance: Shows attention module behavior can be strongly shaped by a few retained tokens, relevant to how context is parameterized and audited.

papers.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
papers.abstract: FlashAttention is an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that computes attention in tiles without materializing the large intermediate attention matrix, using recomputation to cut memory and improve wall-clock speed.
papers.oneLiner: Compute exact attention in tiles, never writing the full attention matrix to HBM, so it is faster and far more memory-efficient.
papers.keyFinding: FlashAttention delivers 2-4x wall-clock speedup and large memory savings, enabling much longer sequence lengths (refined in FlashAttention-2).
papers.weakness: Optimized for GPU HBM/BF16; gains hardware-specific; an implementation improvement, not a change to attention math.
papers.implication: A large part of achievable attention speedup is an I/O and memory-efficiency problem rather than an algorithmic one.
papers.contributions: Tiled exact attention with no intermediate materialization; IO-aware analysis and fused kernels (FlashAttention-2).
papers.methods: Compute softmax in blocks (tiling), online softmax, recomputation to avoid storing the full matrix; fused CUDA kernels.
papers.experiments: GPT-2-style models and others; speed and memory on A100, enabling longer-context training.
papers.results: 2-4x speedup and substantial memory reduction, enabling much larger sequence lengths.
papers.limitations: Hardware-specific; exact same attention; benefits implementation-level.
papers.futureDirections: More hardware, longer contexts, other attention variants.
papers.insights: IO-aware kernel design is a major, largely orthogonal source of LLM speedups.
papers.relevance: Attention-serving efficiency is the baseline every early-exit and dynamic-depth method is compared against.

papers.title: The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers
papers.abstract: Shows that many of the deepest layers of trained LLMs contribute negligibly at inference, and that dropping them with a cheap layer-selection heuristic preserves performance while enabling faster inference (and sometimes improving tasks like MMLU).
papers.oneLiner: Many of an LLM's deepest layers hardly matter, so you can drop them at inference for a nearly-free speedup.
papers.keyFinding: Dropping roughly half the deepest layers of a 70B model gives ~1.5x speedup on a consumer GPU with minimal performance loss; some tasks like MMLU improve.
papers.weakness: Task-dependent; can hurt reasoning/math; simple heuristic selection not always optimal.
papers.implication: Depth-wise redundancy can be exploited for inference-time early exit at nearly zero cost.
papers.contributions: Layer-selection and layer-pruning method; analysis of layer contribution; benchmark across tasks.
papers.methods: Select deeper layers to drop using a proxy measure; evaluate quality against retained depth.
papers.experiments: Llama-2 and Llama-3 up to 70B; quality across tasks and speedup on consumer hardware.
papers.results: ~1.5x speedup from dropping ~50% of layers with minimal loss; MMLU can improve.
papers.limitations: Task-dependent losses; no rigorous per-task optimal policy; heuristic selection.
papers.futureDirections: Better/learned layer-drop policies, per-request dynamic depth, combine with quantization.
papers.insights: Layer redundancy supports cheap inference-time depth control, a direct precedent for early exit.
papers.relevance: Directly relevant to early exit: deciding which layers to drop determines the output changes that must be audited for demographic fairness.

papers.title: BBQ: A Hand-Built Bias Benchmark for Question Answering
papers.abstract: BBQ is a QA benchmark of ~25k questions across nine social-bias categories, each in disambiguated and ambiguous contexts, scoring whether models rely on stereotypes when the answer is not inferable.
papers.oneLiner: A hand-built QA benchmark measuring how strongly LLMs lean on demographic stereotypes by contrasting disambiguated vs ambiguous settings.
papers.keyFinding: Large pretrained QA models show substantial bias in ambiguous contexts (often worse than majority/random baselines), expressed as a large accuracy gap between stereotypic and non-stereotypic answers.
papers.weakness: English QA templates; limited context; ambiguous/abstract items hard to scale.
papers.implication: A model can look 'fair' on unambiguous inputs yet be strongly biased when information is missing, so fairness must be measured in under-determined settings.
papers.contributions: Curated 9-category QA benchmark; bias-score metric netting out accuracy; disambiguated/ambiguous design; leaderboard.
papers.methods: Hand-built contextualized questions with matched candidates; bias score combining ambiguous and disambiguated accuracy.
papers.experiments: GPT-3, RoBERTa, UnifiedQA, BART across all nine categories in both conditions.
papers.results: Large models exhibit accuracy gaps and bias scores well above random in ambiguous items despite high unambiguous accuracy.
papers.limitations: Template-based English-only; may underrepresent cross-cultural and intersectional stereotypes.
papers.futureDirections: Broader demographic coverage, multilingual, open-ended generation.
papers.insights: Bias and raw accuracy must be jointly reported; ambiguous-context behavior isolates stereotype reliance.
papers.relevance: Its accuracy-gap and bias-score framing is the closest template for testing whether an early-exit/adaptive LLM yields unequal QA accuracy across groups.

papers.title: BOLD: Dataset and Metrics for Measuring Biases in Open-Ended Language Generation
papers.abstract: BOLD is a dataset of 23,679 English Wikipedia prompt templates over five domains (gender, race, religion, political affiliation, profession) with five fairness metrics — sentiment, regard, toxicity, gender polarity, word-level similarity.
papers.oneLiner: A large open-ended generation benchmark with concrete per-domain fairness metrics to quantify bias in LLM output text.
papers.keyFinding: Larger models (GPT-2, GPT-3) display more bias in sentiment, regard, and toxicity toward specific groups than smaller ones, with direction/intensity depending on domain.
papers.weakness: Metrics lean on external classifiers with measurement error; coreference/regard judgments can misattribute group sentiment.
papers.implication: Scaling up models is not bias-neutral; quality and 'fairness' signals must be tracked by group during generation.
papers.contributions: 23k-prompt multi-domain corpus; five qualitative fairness metrics; baseline evaluation across models.
papers.methods: Prompt-based open-ended generation from Wikipedia; 'regard' dataset; statistic-based metric set.
papers.experiments: GPT-2/GPT-3 variants; continuations scored by all five metrics across five domains.
papers.results: Sentiment, regard, and toxicity vary systematically by domain and model size, with larger models more biased on several axes.
papers.limitations: English-only Wikipedia prompts; metrics dependent on annotator-based regard labels and classifier thresholds.
papers.futureDirections: Multilingual BOLD; richer metrics; integrating bias metrics into model-selection pipelines.
papers.insights: Group comparisons of generated-text attributes give an operational bridge between 'generation quality' and demographic fairness.
papers.relevance: Supplies per-group sentiment/regard/toxicity metrics to compare whether early-exit LLMs degrade output quality differently across groups.

papers.title: Gender Bias in Coreference Resolution: Evaluation and Debiasing Methods
papers.abstract: Introduces WinoBias, a coreference-resolution dataset built around stereotypical and anti-stereotypical profession/pronoun pairs to expose gender bias, plus two debiasing methods (gender-balanced embeddings and data augmentation).
papers.oneLiner: The canonical gendered coreference benchmark revealing a large performance gap on stereotypical vs anti-stereotypical examples.
papers.keyFinding: Coreference systems perform far worse on anti-stereotypical sentences; data augmentation and gender-balanced embeddings narrow but do not remove the gap.
papers.weakness: Binary-gender framing; English profession/pronoun stimuli; train/test distribution mismatch can inflate apparent bias.
papers.implication: A model's reliability is not uniform across demographic groups — performance can be tied to stereotype conformance.
papers.contributions: WinoBias dataset (stereotypical + anti-stereotypical splits); gender-embedding- and data-based debiasing; empirical analysis.
papers.methods: Two coreference benchmark splits; pronoun-resolution F1-style metric; debiasing via embedding post-processing and data augmentation.
papers.experiments: Several coreference systems (rule-based and neural) on WinoBias with and without debiasing.
papers.results: Consistent performance drop on anti-stereotypical examples; debiasing improves anti-stereotypical accuracy at some cost to overall F1.
papers.limitations: Two genders, English, small dataset; debiasing generalization untested.
papers.futureDirections: Non-binary and intersectional gender; multilingual coreference fairness; downstream transfer of debiasing.
papers.insights: Group-disparity measurement by demographic split is essential even for seemingly 'coreference-only' tasks.
papers.relevance: A classic template for measuring an accuracy/quality disparity between demographic groups — the kind that adaptive inference could introduce or amplify.

papers.title: RealToxicityPrompts: Evaluating Neural Toxic Degeneration in Language Models
papers.abstract: RealToxicityPrompts is a dataset of 100k naturally occurring web prompts whose continuations are scored for toxicity via the Perspective API, documenting 'toxic degeneration' and evaluating filtering, detoxification, and decoding strategies as mitigation.
papers.oneLiner: The standard dataset and framework for measuring and reducing toxic/unsafe outputs in open-ended generation.
papers.keyFinding: Pretrained LMs readily produce toxic continuations from fairly neutral prompts, and toxicity rises with generation length and model size; mitigations reduce but do not eliminate it.
papers.weakness: Toxicity measured by a single external classifier that can itself be biased; prompts are single English web snippets.
papers.implication: Inference-time choices (length, decoding, caching) materially change the risk-profile of generated content, so adaptive inference can shift harm.
papers.contributions: 100k real-prompt corpus; evaluation harness around Perspective API; taxonomy of toxic degeneration and mitigation baselines.
papers.methods: Natural prompt collection; toxicity classifier scoring; perplexity/generation-based filtering; decoding/detoxification baselines.
papers.experiments: GPT-2 variants and other LMs; continuation toxicity under several decoding/filtering settings.
papers.results: Higher toxicity for longer generations and some larger models; mitigations reduce toxicity at a cost to fluency/diversity.
papers.limitations: Toxicity is a narrow harm axis; classifier bias and spurious associations limit precision; no group-level toxicity breakdown.
papers.futureDirections: Beyond toxicity to other harms; per-identity-group toxicity analysis; mitigation downstream cost.
papers.insights: Generation risk depends on inference-time parameters, linking safety metrics to how models are run rather than only trained.
papers.relevance: Shows inference-time behavior (which early-exit changes) alters harm; a natural outcome variable for measuring uneven quality/harm across demographics.

papers.title: StereoSet: Measuring stereotypical bias in pretrained language models
papers.abstract: StereoSet measures stereotypical bias using intrasentence and intersentence contexts across gender, race, religion, and profession, defining a StereoSet Score combining stereotype preference with a language-modeling score.
papers.oneLiner: Introduces the StereoSet Score to quantify a pretrained LM's preference for stereotypical associations while accounting for fluency.
papers.keyFinding: Pretrained models exhibit substantial stereotype preference, and in several cases it increases with model scale/capability.
papers.weakness: Associational (co-occurrence-based) measure that can conflate statistical correlation with genuinely harmful bias; limited to four domains.
papers.implication: Bigger, more capable models are not automatically fairer; bias can scale with capability, so capability gains must be audited separately.
papers.contributions: Intrasentence and intersentence bias datasets; the 'idealized' StereoSet Score combining stereotype preference and LM score; public benchmark.
papers.methods: Candidate-completions scoring; stereotype-preference and LM-score metrics combined into a single score.
papers.experiments: Masked and autoregressive models of multiple sizes on both intrasentence and intersentence sub-tasks.
papers.results: High stereotype preference across models, varying by domain and model class.
papers.limitations: Narrow domains, single target terms, word-association assumptions; low coverage of intersectional identities.
papers.futureDirections: Broader domains/languages; richer harm measures; connecting stereotype score to downstream outcomes.
papers.insights: Bias can be quantified by relative likelihood of stereotypical vs anti-stereotypical completions, a directly reusable scoring recipe.
papers.relevance: The stereotype-preference metric is a direct handle for testing whether an early-exit LLM emits more stereotypical completions when computation is budgeted.

papers.title: CrowS-Pairs: A Challenge Dataset for Measuring Social Biases in Masked Language Models
papers.abstract: CrowS-Pairs is a benchmark of 1,508 minimal sentence pairs (one stereotypical, one anti-stereotypical) across nine bias categories, scored by the relative likelihood a masked LM assigns to the stereotypical sentence.
papers.oneLiner: A minimal-pair benchmark scoring social bias by comparing model likelihood of stereotypical vs anti-stereotypical sentences.
papers.keyFinding: All tested pretrained masked LMs show measurable social bias favoring stereotypical sentences, with magnitude varying by category and model.
papers.weakness: Relies on likelihood differences that engineers can game; sentence-level and English-only; sensitive to template wording.
papers.implication: Bias is present even in models not explicitly designed for generation, and is a property of learned associations, not just decode-time choices.
papers.contributions: 1,508 curated stereotype/anti-stereotype pairs; likelihood-ratio scoring; comparison across many masked LMs.
papers.methods: Pairwise stereotypical vs anti-stereotypical sentences; fraction where the model assigns higher probability to the stereotypical one.
papers.experiments: BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT, and others across all nine categories.
papers.results: All models exhibit bias scores above chance; the degree varies across categories.
papers.limitations: Association-based measure; no downstream/behavioural validation; limited demographic coverage and English-only.
papers.futureDirections: Generative and multilingual models; connect likelihood-based bias to observed behavior and downstream harm.
papers.insights: Minimal-pair likelihood scoring is a lightweight, reproducible way to detect group-based bias.
papers.relevance: A lightweight group-bias probe adaptable to checking whether early-exit thresholds alter the relative likelihood of stereotypical completions.

papers.title: A Group Fairness Lens for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Proposes a group-level fairness framework for LLMs evaluating fairness by comparing the distribution/quality of outputs across demographic groups rather than by a single scalar, arguing group-based comparison reveals disparities masked by pooled scores.
papers.oneLiner: Argues for measuring LLM fairness at the group level across outputs, not with a single aggregate number.
papers.keyFinding: LLMs exhibit measurable group-level disparities in generated-output quality/content that are hidden when only a single pooled fairness value is reported.
papers.weakness: Group definitions and output-level metric choices are modeler-defined; limited to text-generation outputs and English settings.
papers.implication: Reporting only an average fairness score can conceal systematic disadvantage to specific demographic groups.
papers.contributions: Group-level evaluation lens; output-distribution comparison metrics; empirical demonstration of hidden group disparities.
papers.methods: Group-by-group comparison of outputs using distribution-based and quality metrics; fairness-as-group-disparity framing.
papers.experiments: Applies group-level analysis across several LLMs and demographic subgroups on generation tasks.
papers.results: Finds meaningful inter-group disparities in output quality/content that aggregate metrics obscure.
papers.limitations: Group granularity and metric design choices; no standard for choosing grouping; English-centric.
papers.futureDirections: Richer group taxonomies, intersectional groupings, standard output-level fairness metrics.
papers.insights: Group-level comparison is the right unit for catching equity problems that aggregate fairness scores hide.
papers.relevance: Directly supplies the group-disparity evaluation lens to decide whether early-exit LLMs allocate different quality across demographic groups.

papers.title: Measuring Social Biases in Masked Language Models by Proxy of Prediction Quality
papers.abstract: Proposes measuring social bias in masked LMs through per-group prediction quality (accuracy/confidence on tokens associated with different social groups) rather than only through likelihood preference.
papers.oneLiner: Frames bias as a differential in prediction quality/accuracy across social groups, not just association likelihood.
papers.keyFinding: Models show differential prediction quality across demographic group tokens, revealing an accuracy/confidence gap tied to group identity that pure preference measures can miss.
papers.weakness: Requires careful token/group mapping; outcome depends on how groups and target tokens are defined; English-centric.
papers.implication: Bias can be detected as an asymmetric quality/accuracy gap, aligning model fairness with measured capacity rather than sentiment.
papers.contributions: A prediction-quality proxy measure of bias; demonstration that accuracy/confidence gaps differ across groups.
papers.methods: Per-group masked-token prediction tasks; comparing accuracy/confidence across demographic token groups.
papers.experiments: Several masked LMs' group-specific prediction quality on constructed group-targeted stimuli.
papers.results: Reliable group-based prediction-quality gaps across models.
papers.limitations: Proxy measure; sensitivity to stimulus/token selection; not a direct measure of downstream harm.
papers.futureDirections: Link accuracy gaps to downstream behavior; extend to generative LLMs and multilingual settings.
papers.insights: 'Accuracy gap' is a legitimate, measurable fairness signal, not only a sentiment-based notion.
papers.relevance: Provides an accuracy-gap methodology for detecting whether early-exit/adaptive LLMs give different prediction quality to different groups.

papers.title: Quantifying Fairness in LLMs Beyond Tokens: A Semantic and Statistical Perspective
papers.abstract: Proposes augmented fairness metrics at the semantic level (output meaning/similarity) combined with statistical group comparisons, arguing token- and word-level metrics miss semantic disparities in generated content.
papers.oneLiner: Adds semantic-level fairness metrics on top of token/statistical metrics to surface group disparities token measures miss.
papers.keyFinding: Token- and probability-level metrics understate semantic-level differences across groups, so fair-by-token models can still be semantically uneven.
papers.weakness: Relies on semantic-similarity/embedding machinery that can be noisy; group definitions are user-chosen.
papers.implication: Fairness evaluation needs semantic-level measurement; apparent token-level parity can mask unequal meaning quality across groups.
papers.contributions: Semantic + statistical fairness metric set; comparative analysis showing token-level metrics' blind spots.
papers.methods: Combining statistical group comparisons with semantic similarity/embedding distance measures on generated outputs.
