papers.experiments: Applies the augmented metrics across multiple LLMs and demographic groups on generation tasks.
papers.results: Semantic-level metrics reveal larger and qualitatively different group disparities than token-level metrics.
papers.limitations: Dependence on embedding similarity; modeler-defined grouping; English-centric evaluation.
papers.futureDirections: Refined semantic metrics, multilingual coverage, integration with downstream behavior and human audit.
papers.insights: Fairness is a semantic property of outputs, so quality-parity claims must be measured at the meaning level.
papers.relevance: Provides semantic/metric machinery to test whether early-exit LLMs preserve meaning-quality parity across groups, not just token parity.

papers.title: All Should Be Equal in the Eyes of Language Models: Counterfactually Aware Fair Text Generation
papers.abstract: Proposes a counterfactually aware framework for fair text generation: generate counterfactual (group-swapped) inputs and use them to regularize the model so outputs are equally likely and semantically consistent across demographic attributes.
papers.oneLiner: Uses counterfactual group-swapping to make generation equally likely and meaning-preserving across demographic groups.
papers.keyFinding: Counterfactually aware regularization reduces demographic bias while maintaining generation quality and fluency.
papers.weakness: Counterfactual generation limited to salient attributes; requires controllable generation and can distort rare/dependent attributes.
papers.implication: Counterfactual fairness is an achievable target via data/objective engineering, feasible without harming quality much.
papers.contributions: Counterfactual generation pipeline; regularization/training objective for fair generation; empirical bias reduction with quality preservation.
papers.methods: Counterfactual data augmentation via attribute swapping; contrastive/counterfactually-aware training objective; likelihood-balancing regularisation.
papers.experiments: Trains and evaluates generation models on counterfactually augmented data, measuring bias and fluency.
papers.results: Reduced demographic bias with modest impact on generation quality vs strong baselines.
papers.limitations: Attribute scope and counterfactual realism; difficulty swapping non-binary/intersectional attributes.
papers.futureDirections: Richer/intersectional attributes; larger and adaptive models; downstream fairness transfer.
papers.insights: Counterfactual invariance is a principled fairness definition that can be optimized directly.
papers.relevance: Defines a counterfactual-fairness target that early-exit LLMs should ideally preserve, to test whether adaptive inference breaks counterfactual invariance.

papers.title: The Impact of Debiasing on the Performance of Language Models in Downstream Tasks is Underestimated
papers.abstract: Evaluates the true downstream cost of common debiasing methods using broader and more robust performance evaluation, showing the performance/robustness loss from debiasing is larger than standard evaluations report.
papers.oneLiner: Shows that standard debiasing methods hurt downstream performance and robustness more than earlier narrow-task evaluations suggest.
papers.keyFinding: Measured across a broad task suite with robustness awareness, debiasing degrades downstream generalization and robustness substantially more than prior claims.
papers.weakness: Focuses on intrinsic-to-extrinsic transfer and named debiasing methods; generalization to generative/RLHF-style LLMs limited.
papers.implication: Debiasing is not free: removing bias can reduce quality/capability, so fairness and capability must be jointly optimized.
papers.contributions: Broad empirical comparison of debiasing methods; robustness-aware downstream evaluation; evidence costs are underestimated.
papers.methods: Applies multiple established debiasing methods; evaluates on a large downstream task suite with performance and robustness metrics.
papers.experiments: Systematically compares debiasing methods across many downstream tasks and robustness measures.
papers.results: Debiasing reduces downstream performance/robustness more than prior narrow evaluations indicated; trade-off varies by method.
papers.limitations: Task-suite and metric choices; English-centric; limited to a specific set of debiasing techniques and model sizes.
papers.futureDirections: Approaches improving fairness without degrading capability; adaptive and post-hoc debiasing.
papers.insights: Any fairness intervention has a capability cost, so fairness evaluations must also report downstream quality.
papers.relevance: Frames the fairness-vs-capability trade-off that adaptive/early-exit inference also faces: budgeted compute may buy fairness or capability, sometimes at each other's expense.

papers.title: Selecting Shots for Demographic Fairness in Few-Shot Learning with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Studies how the composition and selection of in-context examples (shots) in few-shot LLM learning affects downstream demographic fairness, proposing strategies to select demographically balanced demonstrations.
papers.oneLiner: Shows the demographic makeup of in-context examples drives downstream group fairness and that balanced-shot selection helps.
papers.keyFinding: The demographic distribution of selected shots strongly shapes fairness outcomes; selecting balanced shots improves fairness without significantly hurting accuracy.
papers.weakness: Limited to few-shot in-context learning and a specific set of attributes/tasks; shot-selection search cost.
papers.implication: Inference-time composition of the prompt — analogous to how adaptive inference composes computation — is a controllable lever on group fairness.
papers.contributions: Empirical study of shot-selection and fairness; balanced-shot selection strategy; analysis across demographic attributes.
papers.methods: In-context-example composition experiments; demographic-balance-aware shot selection vs baselines.
papers.experiments: Classification and QA-style few-shot tasks across models, varying demographic composition of demonstrations.
papers.results: Balanced shot selection yields fairness gains with marginal accuracy change vs unconstrained selection.
papers.limitations: Few-shot/labeled-demo paradigm; some attributes; English tasks; limited breadth.
papers.futureDirections: Larger/shared models, other languages, intersectional attributes, adaptive inference settings.
papers.insights: What an LLM is given — including demographic composition — determines whether it behaves equitably across groups.
papers.relevance: Shows inference-time composition (by analogy, early-exit/budget decisions) is a fairness lever, informing whether adaptive LLMs can be tuned to keep groups equal.

papers.title: Pruning has a disparate impact on model accuracy
papers.abstract: Shows that standard magnitude-based pruning degrades accuracy far more severely for minority/underrepresented groups than for majority groups, so compression introduces or amplifies group disparity; proposes a constrained pruning formulation.
papers.oneLiner: Magnitude pruning disproportionately hurts minority subgroups' accuracy, so the compressed model is less fair than its dense counterpart.
papers.keyFinding: Aggressive pruning produces unequal accuracy loss across demographics, with underrepresented groups bearing a larger drop, even when overall (average) accuracy is preserved.
papers.weakness: Vision classifiers and a single pruning heuristic; accuracy-parity metric; mitigation adds optimization cost.
papers.implication: An efficiency transform that looks 'fair' on mean accuracy can be systematically unfair to minority groups, so compression must be audited per-group.
papers.contributions: Casts pruning under group-difference constraints; demonstrates disparate impact; proposes constrained pruning for accuracy parity.
papers.methods: Magnitude pruning with a constrained optimization step enforcing across-group accuracy differences below a threshold.
papers.experiments: Image classification with multiple pruning rates and datasets with known demographic/skin-tone grouping; sparse vs dense per-group accuracy.
papers.results: Per-group accuracy gaps widen with sparsity; the constrained method closes much of the gap at modest pruning cost.
papers.limitations: Vision-centric; sensitivity to subgroup definitions; does not address other sensitive attributes or sequence models.
papers.futureDirections: Extend to language/VLM models, other pruning criteria, causal explanation of which weights hurt minority groups.
papers.insights: Pruning is not fairness-neutral: accuracy parity should be reported per subgroup, and compression budgets interact with group vulnerability.
papers.relevance: Directly the closest analog to early-exit LLMs: an efficiency transform preserving average quality but redistributing error onto minority groups, motivating subgroup-level auditing of dynamic exits.

papers.title: A Fair Loss Function for Network Pruning
papers.abstract: Introduces a fairness-aware loss added during pruning so the pruned network does not diverge in performance across demographic groups, reporting balanced AUC-ROC across skin tones even under heavy pruning.
papers.oneLiner: Adding a fairness loss during pruning keeps accuracy balanced across skin tones instead of letting AUC-ROC drift apart.
papers.keyFinding: Pruning alone causes divergent AUC-ROC across dark vs light skin tones; a fair pruning loss eliminates that divergence while preserving sparsity.
papers.weakness: Face/skin-tone centric; fairness term is a heuristic loss weight; narrow classifier and dataset.
papers.implication: The pruning objective itself is the correct place to inject fairness, rather than post-hoc rebalancing of the sparse model.
papers.contributions: A novel additive fair loss for the pruning objective; empirical demonstration of balanced AUC across groups post-pruning.
papers.methods: Magnitude/gradient-based pruning with a fairness penalty added to the loss; comparison of pruned models with and without the fair term.
papers.experiments: Face attribute classifier at several pruning ratios; AUC-ROC by skin-tone group.
papers.results: Baseline pruning shows divergent subgroup AUC; adding the fair loss yields near-parity subgroup AUC at comparable sparsity.
papers.limitations: Narrow domain; single-protected-attribute setting; no theoretical guarantee of the fair term.
papers.futureDirections: Generalize to language models, multiple/intersectional attributes, other compression (quantization, distillation).
papers.insights: Fairness can be engineered into the compression cost function itself, transferable to training early-exit LLMs with exit-specific fairness penalties.
papers.relevance: Encapsulates how to make an efficiency transform fairness-aware during the compression step — analogous to making an early-exit policy fairness-aware at training time.

papers.title: Coupling Fairness and Pruning in a Single Run: a Bi-level Optimization Perspective
papers.abstract: Formulates fairness-preserving pruning as a bi-level optimization that jointly decides which weights to drop and enforces a fairness constraint (e.g., equalized odds), asking how to make a compressed model fair in one run.
papers.oneLiner: Pruning and fairness are solved together as a single bi-level problem, so the sparse model satisfies both sparsity and group-fairness goals.
papers.keyFinding: Treating fairness as a constraint inside a bi-level optimization lets pruning reach high sparsity without sacrificing equalized-odds across groups, outperforming post-hoc pruning-then-rebalancing.
papers.weakness: Optimization more expensive and hyperparameter-sensitive; uses standard fairness benchmarks instead of LLM/foundation-model settings.
papers.implication: Compression and fairness should be co-optimized, not sequential, because pruning first and correcting later tends to entrench disparity.
papers.contributions: Bi-level formulation coupling sparsity and fairness; algorithm to solve in a single run; theoretical and empirical analyses.
papers.methods: Bi-level optimization with inner sparsity/pruning and outer fairness constraint; gradient-based alternating updates.
papers.experiments: Multiple datasets and sensitive attributes; sparsity vs equalized odds; compares with fairness-agnostic and sequential baselines.
papers.results: Maintains fairness at high sparsity, beating sequential approaches and pruning baselines on group-accuracy and equalized-odds metrics.
papers.limitations: Optimization overhead; sensitivity to constraint weights; not yet on large transformer/LLM models.
papers.futureDirections: Scale to LLMs, integrate with distillation, study growth of disparity with sparsity.
papers.insights: Fairness-constrained joint optimization is a principled way to make any compression (or early-exit) transform group-aware.
papers.relevance: Provides the optimization machinery to add a demographic-fairness constraint when training early-exit heads, rather than auditing exits after the fact.

papers.title: FairGRAPE: Fairness-aware GRAdient Pruning mEthod for Face Attribute Classification
papers.abstract: Proposes a gradient-based pruning criterion that is fairness-aware for face attribute classification, so pruning keeps accuracy balanced across demographic groups while reducing computation.
papers.oneLiner: A fairness-aware gradient-pruning criterion prunes networks for face attributes without worsening demographic imbalance.
papers.keyFinding: Using a fairness-aware ranking of gradients (rather than plain magnitude) preserves demographic parity and individual fairness while pruning.
papers.weakness: Face-specific; limited to attribute classification and one fairness metric; assumes well-annotated group labels.
papers.implication: The criterion by which weights are pruned is itself a fairness lever; blind magnitude pruning can select the weights that protect minority groups.
papers.contributions: Fairness-aware gradient pruning method; empirical comparison against magnitude and other gradient-based pruning on face attributes.
papers.methods: Gradient-based pruning weighted by a fairness-aware term; pruning without retraining plus optional fine-tuning.
papers.experiments: Face attribute classification at multiple sparsity levels; fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds) per attribute.
papers.results: Achieves comparable sparsity with better fairness outcomes than magnitude pruning, reducing group-accuracy spread.
papers.limitations: Domain-limited; needs sensitive attributes; fairness metric choice affects measured parity.
papers.futureDirections: Apply fairness-aware criterion to transformer models and text/LLM compression.
papers.insights: Choosing which weights to remove is a fairness decision; even a single pruning-criterion change alters demographic outcomes.
papers.relevance: Demonstrates that the pruning criterion — the analogue of an early-exit confidence rule — can be tuned to protect minority groups.

papers.title: Balancing Act: Constraining Disparate Impact in Sparse Models
papers.abstract: Develops a method to enforce sparsity and a disparate-impact (fairness) constraint simultaneously, producing sparse models that are both compact and fair, with a principled framework to trade off sparsity vs fairness.
papers.oneLiner: Sparsity and disparate-impact constraints are enforced together, giving sparse models that stay fair by construction.
papers.keyFinding: One can attain high sparsity while holding disparate impact near the pre-pruning level, but there is a real sparsity-versus-fairness trade-off a joint method navigates far better than post-hoc corrections.
papers.weakness: Constrained optimization adds cost; benchmark-centered; guarantee depends on reliable group labels.
papers.implication: Sparse-model fairness must be a hard constraint during training/compression, not an afterthought, and comes at a measurable sparsity cost.
papers.contributions: Joint sparsity + disparate-impact constrained objective; empirical study of the sparsity/fairness Pareto frontier.
papers.methods: Sparse training/compression with an explicit disparate-impact constraint solved via constrained optimization.
papers.experiments: Multiple tabular and image datasets; accuracy, sparsity, disparate impact together; Pareto curves.
papers.results: Joint method keeps disparate impact low at high sparsity where fairness-agnostic pruning fails, at modest accuracy cost.
papers.limitations: Requires sensitive attributes; constrained solver overhead; not on large-scale LLMs.
papers.futureDirections: Apply to transformers/LLMs; explore fairness metrics beyond disparate impact and intersectional groups.
papers.insights: There is an explicit accuracy/sparsity/fairness trade-off surface that compression systems should expose rather than hide.
papers.relevance: Introduces the trade-off framing essential for early-exit LLMs: each exit threshold is a compression knob tunable against a fairness constraint.

papers.title: Fair Scratch Tickets: Finding Fair Sparse Networks without Weight Training
papers.abstract: Extends the lottery-ticket hypothesis to fairness, searching for fair sparse subnetworks ('fair scratch tickets') that are both accurate and fair without weight training, using a fairness-aware weight importance.
papers.oneLiner: Fair, sparse winning tickets exist and can be identified in one shot without training, when importance is scored by a fairness-aware criterion.
papers.keyFinding: Iterative magnitude pruning using a fairness-aware importance score finds sparse subnetworks that preserve (or improve) fairness while retaining accuracy.
papers.weakness: Dataset/domain specific (image classification); fairness depends on the chosen importance metric and annotation; no large-transformer scaling.
papers.implication: Fairness can be embedded in the selection of a sparse subnetwork at initialization, so compression need not be a fairness tax if the right subnetwork is chosen.
papers.contributions: Defines 'fair scratch tickets'; a fair-network-matching importance criterion; one-shot search for fair sparse networks without retraining.
papers.methods: Lottery-ticket-style iterative/pruned subnetwork search with a fairness-aware weight importance criterion.
papers.experiments: Image classification benchmarks across demographics; fair vs standard scratch tickets and dense baselines.
papers.results: Fair scratch tickets match or beat accuracy of random/dense baselines while improving demographic parity; findable without weight training.
papers.limitations: Requires group annotations; domain-limited; quality depends on initialization and task.
papers.futureDirections: Scale to LLMs and text; fair tickets for quantization and distillation; intersectional groups.
papers.insights: The initial sparse structure, not only training, determines fairness — relevant for pre-selecting fair early-exit heads.
papers.relevance: Shows a sparse-subnetwork (compressed) model can be fair by construction at initialization, analogous to choosing a fair early-exit subnetwork.

papers.title: You Never Know: Quantization Induces Inconsistent Biases in Vision-Language Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Systematically studies how quantization affects bias in multimodal vision-language foundation models, finding its impact is neither consistent nor uniform across models, tasks, and precision; some settings amplify bias, others reduce it.
papers.oneLiner: Quantization's effect on multimodal bias is inconsistent across models and precision, so it cannot be assumed harmful or harmless.
papers.keyFinding: Quantization-induced bias changes vary in direction and magnitude across vision-language models and bit-widths, so no single 'quantization hurts fairness' claim holds.
papers.weakness: Multimodal scope; bias measured with a limited set of social-bias benchmarks; no consistent predictive rule.
papers.implication: Fairness audits of quantized foundation models must be per-model and per-precision, since aggregate assumptions mislead.
papers.contributions: Broad empirical study of quantization's non-uniform bias impact on vision-language models; identification of inconsistent bias shifts.
papers.methods: Post-training quantization at multiple bit-widths; social-bias metrics before/after across many VLMs and tasks.
papers.experiments: Multiple vision-language foundation models and precision levels; bias metrics pre- and post-quantization.
papers.results: Bias changes direction with model and bit-width; some models become more biased, others less; trends non-monotonic.
papers.limitations: No causal/attribution mechanism; benchmark/dataset limits; mainly vision-language rather than text-only LLMs.
papers.futureDirections: Predictors/explainers of which models become biased; extend to text-only LLMs and reasoning; investigate mitigations.
papers.insights: Compression fairness is model- and precision-dependent, arguing for cheap per-model fairness auditing during deployment.
papers.relevance: Strongly parallels early-exit LLM fairness: the same efficiency transform changes bias in complex, non-obvious ways across models.

papers.title: How Quantization Shapes Bias in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Investigates how quantization influences social bias in LLMs across different demographic subgroups, model architectures, and reasoning capability levels; finds quantization shifts bias in subgroup-specific and architecture-dependent ways.
papers.oneLiner: Quantization reshapes LLM social bias unevenly across demographic subgroups and architectures, so bias cannot be assumed constant under compression.
papers.keyFinding: Quantization affects subgroups differently, and the direction/scale of bias change depends on model architecture and reasoning capability, complicating safe deployment.
papers.weakness: Text-bias benchmarks may not capture real harm; findings descriptive without a corrective method.
papers.implication: Deploying quantized LLMs requires subgroup-level bias checks, because the compressed model may quietly become more biased toward specific groups.
papers.contributions: A systematic cross-architecture, cross-subgroup study of quantization's effect on LLM social bias; released code.
papers.methods: Post-training quantization to multiple precisions; subgroup-disaggregated bias metrics across models and reasoning settings.
papers.experiments: Many open LLMs, multiple bit-widths, subgroup-disaggregated bias metrics, reasoning-task comparisons.
papers.results: Bias changes are heterogeneous: some subgroups get worse, some better, and patterns differ by architecture and precision.
papers.limitations: Benchmark-driven bias measures; LLM fairness metrics debated; no mitigation proposed.
papers.futureDirections: Bias-preserving post-processing, subgroup-aware quantization, intersectional analysis.
papers.insights: For LLM compression, fairness is non-monotonic across subgroups — a direct lesson for early-exit LLM deployment.
papers.relevance: The most directly relevant analog: an efficiency transform (here quantization) changing subgroup-level bias of language models.

papers.title: Fair-GPTQ: Bias-Aware Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Proposes a bias-aware quantization method for LLMs that incorporates fairness awareness into the quantization objective, so the compressed model retains better demographic balance, building on GPTQ-style quantization.
papers.oneLiner: A GPTQ-style quantizer made bias-aware, so LLM quantization no longer trades away fairness.
papers.keyFinding: Injecting a fairness-aware term into the quantization calibration substantially reduces compression-induced bias growth compared to standard GPTQ at the same bit-width.
papers.weakness: Adds calibration overhead; fairness evaluated on benchmark probes rather than real-world harm; limited model set.
papers.implication: Fairness can be engineered directly into the compression (quantization) algorithm, preserving balance at little cost in accuracy.
papers.contributions: A bias-aware quantization objective on top of GPTQ; empirical comparison against standard quantization on LLM fairness benchmarks.
papers.methods: GPTQ-style post-training quantization with an added fairness/anchoring term during weight-update calibration.
papers.experiments: Multiple open LLMs at several bit-widths; fairness and perplexity/accuracy vs standard GPTQ and other quantizers.
papers.results: Reduces quantization-induced bias at small fidelity cost, beating fairness-agnostic quantizers on subgroup fairness.
papers.limitations: Benchmark-based fairness; overhead; sensitive to fairness anchor; not tested at very low bit-widths.
papers.futureDirections: Very low precision, integrate pruning+quantization, measure downstream-task fairness.
papers.insights: Fairness-aware compression objectives can be built into low-bit quantizers — a template for bias-aware efficiency transforms.
papers.relevance: Shows a concrete recipe for making a compression/efficiency transform (quantization) bias-aware, transferable to early-exit LLM design.

papers.title: Explaining How Quantization Disparately Skews a Model
papers.abstract: Provides a mechanism/attribution framework for why quantization disparately skews model predictions across groups, decomposing the error introduced by quantization by input/sample characteristics.
papers.oneLiner: Identifies and attributes the mechanism by which quantization disproportionately distorts certain groups' predictions.
papers.keyFinding: Quantization error is unevenly distributed, and specific per-sample/per-group features explain why some groups' outputs are skewed far more than others.
papers.weakness: Focuses on explanation with less mitigation; attribution relies on interpretability proxies that can be imperfect.
papers.implication: Understanding which inputs/features drive quantization skew enables targeted fixes (better rounding for those samples) rather than blanket re-quantization.
papers.contributions: A decomposition/attribution framework explaining quantization's disparate group skew; empirical validation of the mechanism.
papers.methods: Attribution/influence analysis of quantization error across groups; feature- and sample-level error decomposition.
papers.experiments: Quantized vision/language models with grouped samples; show which sample features drive large group-specific error.
papers.results: Identifies a small set of driving features/samples accounting for most of the group skew; supports targeted mitigation.
papers.limitations: Interpretability-limited; case-study scale; may not generalize across all model families.
papers.futureDirections: Turn explanations into corrective quantization schemes; generalize to text LLMs and combined compression; intersectional attributes.
papers.insights: Explaining WHY compression hurts a group enables fixes — not just demonstrating that it does.
papers.relevance: For early-exit LLMs, provides explanatory tools to diagnose which inputs/samples the efficiency transform most distorts per group.

papers.title: RELIANT: Fair Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Introduces a fairness-aware knowledge distillation approach for graph neural networks so the distilled (smaller) student stays fair even when the teacher is biased, balancing performance, complexity, and fairness.
papers.oneLiner: A distillation loss that propagates fairness to a compact student, keeping compressed students group-fair.
papers.keyFinding: Naive distillation inherits (and can amplify) teacher bias; adding a fairness-aware distillation objective yields fair, compact students without much accuracy loss.
papers.weakness: Graph/transductive domain; requires an available teacher; fairness measured on graph node attributes.
papers.implication: Distillation — a model-reduction transform — is a vector for bias transfer, so the student objective must explicitly enforce fairness.
papers.contributions: A fair distillation loss for GNNs; experiments on accuracy vs fairness under distillation; analysis of bias transfer through compression.
papers.methods: Knowledge distillation with an added fairness-aware loss (demographic parity / equalized odds) between teacher and student.
papers.experiments: GNN classification on datasets with sensitive node attributes; compare distilled students with/without fair loss.
papers.results: Fair-aware distillation yields students with parity close to the teacher at a fraction of complexity, vs biased naive-distilled students.
papers.limitations: Graph-specific; single protected attribute; requires annotated sensitive labels.
papers.futureDirections: Extend to transformer/LLM distillation, multiple attributes, label-unknown scenarios.
papers.insights: Compression by distillation does not inherit fairness for free — the student objective must be made fairness-aware.
papers.relevance: Mirrors the teacher→student bias-transfer question for early-exit nets, where small exit heads distill the backbone's behavior (and biases).

papers.title: What Is Left After Distillation? How Knowledge Transfer Impacts Fairness and Bias
papers.abstract: Empirically studies how knowledge distillation affects fairness and bias, showing distillation can substantially change (and sometimes amplify) bias depending on teacher, student, and training setup; questions the assumption distillation is fairness-neutral.
papers.oneLiner: Distillation is not fairness-neutral — it can amplify or reduce bias depending on teacher/student and settings.
papers.keyFinding: Distilling a teacher into a smaller student shifts bias meaningfully, and the direction depends on distillation hyperparameters, teacher bias, and student capacity.
papers.weakness: Descriptive, benchmark-driven; bias metrics are limited proxies; no corrective method proposed.
papers.implication: Model reduction via distillation must be audited for fairness, because the smaller model can carry more (not less) bias than the teacher.
papers.contributions: A systematic study of distillation's effect on fairness/bias across NLP settings; causal attribution to teacher and distillation choices.
papers.methods: Train teachers and distill into students across settings; measure NLP fairness/bias probes before/after distillation.
papers.experiments: Multiple language models/teachers, students, and distillation configurations; compare bias metrics to teacher baseline.
papers.results: Distillation changes bias in both directions; certain student/temperature settings amplify bias while others reduce it.
papers.limitations: NLP-benchmark bias measures; no mitigation; may not cover larger modern LLMs.
papers.futureDirections: Bias-aware distillation for LLMs; combined compression pipelines; intersectional fairness.
papers.insights: Every model-reduction step (distillation) is a point where fairness can drift; treat compression as a multi-stage fairness risk.
papers.relevance: Directly relevant: exit heads effectively distill the backbone's outputs, so their bias must be audited separately.

papers.title: Characterising Bias in Compressed Models
papers.abstract: Examines how compression (pruning, quantization, distillation) interacts with fairness, showing that compressed models can disproportionately degrade underrepresented groups and that the effect is a function of the compression technique and group.
papers.oneLiner: Compression does not affect all groups equally, so compressed models can be less fair than the originals.
papers.keyFinding: Distillation and pruning at aggressive rates disproportionately hurt underrepresented groups even when average performance is maintained, and the bias depends on the compression method.
papers.weakness: Focuses on standard compression methods and a set of benchmarks; group definitions and bias metrics limit scope.
papers.implication: Compression is a fairness risk even when it preserves mean accuracy, so subgroup-level auditing is required for any model-reduction technique.
papers.contributions: Early systematic evidence that compression amplifies group disparity; characterization across compression methods; discussion of mitigation.
papers.methods: Prune/quantize/distill models and measure per-group accuracy and fairness metrics; compare against dense baselines.
papers.experiments: Multiple vision/NLP models and compression rates; per-group (subgroup) accuracy and fairness metrics.
papers.results: Compressed models show larger performance gaps across groups, with the effect depending on the compression technique and rate.
papers.limitations: Benchmark-limited; pre-dates large LLMs; no causal mechanism for which weights hurt groups.
papers.futureDirections: Extend to LLM compression and adaptive/dynamic inference; explain mechanism; fairness-aware compression.
papers.insights: Bias amplification is a general property of compression, not specific to one method.
papers.relevance: Foundational evidence that efficiency transforms (the class early-exit belongs to) can be fairness-detrimental, motivating group-level auditing.

papers.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks: Temperature Scaling
papers.abstract: Shows that modern neural networks are typically overconfident and miscalibrated, and introduces temperature scaling — a simple post-hoc transform of logits that markedly improves calibration.
papers.oneLiner: Introduces temperature scaling as a simple, effective post-hoc calibration method for modern neural nets.
papers.keyFinding: Modern networks are overconfident (poor ECE), and a single temperature parameter learned on validation data substantially recalibrates them, better than Platt or binning in many settings.
papers.weakness: Post-hoc on validation data; a single global temperature is not group- or input-conditional; assumes a well-defined label distribution.
papers.implication: Confidence scores are systematically miscalibrated, so any threshold on confidence (e.g., early exit) inherits that miscalibration.
papers.contributions: Empirical demonstration of overconfidence; the temperature-scaling method; comparison against alternative calibration methods.
papers.methods: Temperature scaling (T), ensemble/temperature variants; evaluated with ECE and reliability diagrams.
papers.experiments: ImageNet classification with modern CNN/ResNet models; ECE and calibration curves.
papers.results: Temperature scaling reduces ECE substantially, being the most robust simple post-hoc calibrator.
papers.limitations: Global scalar; validation-dependent; may not generalize across domains or groups.
papers.futureDirections: Per-group / per-context temperature; calibration under label ambiguity; LLM calibration.
papers.insights: Confidence is not trustworthy without calibration, so confidence-based decisions need a calibration step.
papers.relevance: Grounds the calibration-disparity mechanism: if temperature/confidence reliability differs across groups, a shared exit threshold exits at different true-error levels.

papers.title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
papers.abstract: Empirically evaluates how well LLMs can express uncertainty (verbalized confidence, sampling-based, verbalized-probability), finding significant overconfidence and poor failure prediction in vanilla confidence elicitation.
papers.oneLiner: LLM verbalized confidence exhibits substantial overconfidence and poor failure prediction, casting doubt on its reliability.
papers.keyFinding: Vanilla verbalized confidence is overconfident and unreliable for detecting wrong answers; certain prompting/self-consistency methods improve uncertainty estimation but not to a reliable degree.
papers.weakness: Evaluates a limited set of elicitation strategies and tasks; confidence is not fully calibrated without post-processing.
papers.implication: Since LLM confidence is unreliable, any confidence-driven early-exit decision has an uncertain basis, which could differ by input/group.
papers.contributions: Systematic empirical comparison of confidence-elicitation methods for LLM failure/uncertainty estimation.
papers.methods: Verbalized confidence, sampling-based self-consistency, verbalized probability across question-answering tasks; AUC/ECE-style eval.
papers.experiments: Multiple LLMs on QA/classification tasks; uncertainty-estimation quality (AUROC, calibration).
papers.results: Under self-consistency, larger models are better calibrated and more accurate, but most show overconfidence; confidence poorly predicts correctness.
papers.limitations: Task/elicitation-limited; calibration not group-disaggregated; English-centric.
papers.futureDirections: Group-wise calibration; calibrated selective prediction; better uncertainty for LLM agents.
papers.insights: LLM confidence is not a reliable stand-in for correctness, so early-exit 'confidence' signals must be calibrated.
papers.relevance: Directly supports the calibration-disparity hypothesis: if confidence reliability differs across groups, confidence-based early exit yields unequal quality.

papers.title: Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation in Natural Language Generation
papers.abstract: Introduces semantic entropy: cluster sampled generations by meaning (via entailment) and compute entropy over semantic equivalence classes, giving a way to estimate uncertainty in open-ended generation.
papers.oneLiner: Aggregate sampling entropy over meaning-equivalent outputs to estimate generation uncertainty.
papers.keyFinding: Semantic entropy better distinguishes correct from incorrect generations than token-level metrics, improving selective prediction and could reduce hallucination risk.
papers.weakness: Requires multiple samples and an entailment model; relies on the meaning-partitioning assumption; cost is high.
papers.implication: Token-level confidence is a poor proxy for generation uncertainty; meaning-aware uncertainty is more reliable.
papers.contributions: Semantic-entropy estimator; meaning-clustering via entailment; application to selective prediction/QA.
papers.methods: Sample multiple generations; cluster by meaning (entailment); compute entropy over clusters; use for uncertainty/selective prediction.
papers.experiments: Open-ended QA/generation; uncertainty-quality (AUROC) and selective-prediction performance.
papers.results: Semantic entropy yields better uncertainty than token-level metrics and improves abstention/selective prediction.
papers.limitations: Sampling+entailment cost; meaning clustering can be imperfect; not group-disaggregated.
papers.futureDirections: Efficient semantic uncertainty; calibrated confidence for generation; group-level uncertainty auditing.
papers.insights: Uncertainty in generation is a property of meaning, not just token probability.
papers.relevance: If generation-uncertainty is meaning-based and differs across groups, then early-exit confidence (often token-level) may mis-rank groups.

papers.title: Thermometer: Towards Universal Calibration for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Proposes a universal calibration method (Thermometer) that calibrates LLMs across tasks and input distributions using a small set of labeled data, addressing the task-specificity of temperature scaling.
papers.oneLiner: A universal calibrator that works across tasks and distributions, avoiding per-task temperature tuning.
papers.keyFinding: Thermometer generalizes temperature-scaling-style calibration across tasks, achieving better calibration with fewer labels and being robust to distribution shift.
papers.weakness: Requires some labeled data; may not fully capture uncertainty in open-ended generation; calibration quality depends on calibration set.
papers.implication: Calibration can be made task- and distribution-agnostic, but the calibration data composition (and any group skew) still matters.
papers.contributions: A universal calibration framework; method that generalizes across tasks; improved calibration under distribution shift.
papers.methods: Learns a calibration function/parameterization that transfers across tasks; evaluated with ECE.
papers.experiments: Multiple LLM tasks and distributions; calibration error and sample efficiency vs temperature scaling.
papers.results: Better calibration and robustness across tasks than per-task temperature scaling, with fewer labels.
papers.limitations: Needs calibration data; not group-disaggregated; generation-setting applicability depends on the calibration distribution.
papers.futureDirections: Group-aware and distribution-robust calibration; calibration for generation; uncertainty-aware decoding.
papers.insights: Calibration is not one-size-fits-all but can be made transferable; the calibration data distribution determines its fairness.
papers.relevance: Supports per-group calibrated confidence as a route to fair early-exit thresholds, and warns that calibration data must be representative.

papers.title: Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words
papers.abstract: Trains a model (T5) to express uncertainty in words given a question and a set of sampled answers, so the model can verbalize calibrated-confidence answers.
papers.oneLiner: Fine-tune a model to verbalize calibrated confidence about its sampled answers.
papers.keyFinding: Trained verbalized confidence is better calibrated and more accurate than a baseline, improving calibration and selective prediction.
papers.weakness: Requires sampled answers; verbalization is not fully reliable for very open tasks; not group-disaggregated.
papers.implication: Confidence can be learned as a first-class output rather than derived from logits, offering a controllable uncertainty signal for exit decisions.
papers.contributions: A training approach to verbalized uncertainty; improved calibration and selective prediction in NLG.
papers.methods: Fine-tune sequence-to-sequence model to append confidence phrase given question + sample set; evaluate calibration.
papers.experiments: NLG/QA tasks; calibration and selective-prediction metrics vs baselines.
papers.results: Verbalized confidence improves calibration relative to untrained baselines and is usable for abstention.
papers.limitations: Needs a sampled candidate set; verbalization biased by the model; no group-level calibration.
papers.futureDirections: Trustworthy verbalized uncertainty; group-wise calibration; integration into agents/systems.
papers.insights: Confidence can be explicitly trained, providing a controllable signal for adaptive decisions.
papers.relevance: Suggests an alternative to raw logit confidence for early-exit decisions — a trainable, potentially group-calibrated signal.

papers.title: Entropy Alone is Insufficient for Safe Selective Prediction in LLMs
papers.abstract: Argues that entropy-based uncertainty is insufficient for safe selective prediction/abstention in LLMs, and that additional signals (e.g., semantic, self-consistency, calibration-aware) are needed.
papers.oneLiner: Shows entropy is not a safe standalone signal for when LLMs should abstain or be trusted.
papers.keyFinding: Low-entropy high-confidence outputs can still be wrong, so entropy alone is not a safe abstention/trust signal.
papers.weakness: Entropy is a single-uncertainty proxy; findings depend on task and model; framing is empiricist.
papers.implication: Early-exit decisions based purely on entropy (or confidence) may be unsafe, since low-uncertainty tokens can still be incorrect.
papers.contributions: Evidence that entropy-based selective prediction is not safe; analysis of failure modes; call for additional uncertainty signals.
papers.methods: Compare entropy vs alternative uncertainty signals; measure selective-prediction performance (AUROC/risk-coverage).
papers.experiments: Several LLMs on generation/QA; risk-coverage and selective-prediction metrics.
papers.results: Entropy-based abstention is unsafe; adding semantic/self-consistency signals improves coverage at equal risk.
papers.limitations: Entropy proxy-centric; limited signal set; not group-disaggregated.
papers.futureDirections: Multi-signal uncertainty; calibrated and group-aware selective prediction.
papers.insights: Confidence/entropy alone are insufficient to guarantee correctness — a caution for entropy-based early exit.
papers.relevance: Warns that entropy thresholds (a common early-exit rule) are not sufficient to ensure quality parity across groups.

papers.title: Revisiting Uncertainty Estimation and Calibration of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Re-examines uncertainty estimation and calibration for LLMs, comparing methods and finding that calibration and uncertainty-quality are model- and task-dependent, with implications for reliable confidence.
papers.oneLiner: Reassesses LLM uncertainty/calibration across methods and models, showing dependency on model and task.
papers.keyFinding: Uncertainty-estimation quality and calibration vary substantially across methods, models, and tasks, and are rarely reliable enough for risk-sensitive decisions.
papers.weakness: Descriptive; relies on calibration/uncertainty proxies; limited corrective method.
papers.implication: Portable, reliable confidence for LLMs remains unsolved, so decisions on confidence (e.g., early exit) need per-model auditing.
papers.contributions: Broad comparison of LLM uncertainty/calibration methods; characterization of reliability across models/tasks.
papers.methods: Compare multiple uncertainty/calibration estimators; measure calibration error and uncertainty quality across models/tasks.
papers.experiments: Multiple LLMs and tasks; ECE/AUROC-style metrics.
papers.results: Reliability is heterogeneous; no single method is consistently well calibrated across models/tasks.
papers.limitations: Metrics and task set limited; no group-disaggregated or intersectional analysis.
papers.futureDirections: Task/model-adaptive calibration; trustworthy confidence for decision-making; group-aware analysis.
papers.insights: Confidence reliability is not portable — it must be validated per model and task (and per group).
papers.relevance: Underlines that exit-threshold confidence must be validated per model, task, and group to avoid unfair early-exit outcomes.

papers.title: The Art of Abstention: Selective Prediction and Error Regularization for Natural Language Processing
papers.abstract: Studies selective prediction (abstention) in NLP with a calibration-aware error-regularization training objective, improving the model's ability to abstain when uncertain and improving the risk-coverage trade-off.
papers.oneLiner: A training objective that improves selective prediction (abstention) and the risk-coverage trade-off in NLP.
papers.keyFinding: Error-regularized selective prediction substantially improves risk-coverage and calibration, enabling models to abstain on hard inputs while preserving accuracy on confident ones.
papers.weakness: Focuses on classification-style NLP; abstention metrics may not map to generation; no group-level abstention analysis.
papers.implication: Selective prediction gives a principled lever for compute-and-answer decisions; how well it abstains per group is a fairness question.
papers.contributions: An error-regularization objective for selective prediction; analysis of risk-coverage and calibration in NLP.
papers.methods: Train with an additional calibration/error-regularization term; measure risk-coverage and calibration.
papers.experiments: NLP classification tasks; risk-coverage, AUROC, calibration metrics.
papers.results: Better risk-coverage and calibration than standard training; effective abstention on hard instances.
papers.limitations: Classification-centric; not group-disaggregated; abstraction/abstention metric choices.
papers.futureDirections: Extend to generation/LLMs; group-aware abstention; combine with early exit.
papers.insights: Selective prediction is the decision-theoretic cousin of early exit, and its calibration is critical for fairness.
papers.relevance: Provides the selective-prediction machinery to test whether a model abstains (exits) differently across demographic groups.

papers.title: Calibrated Uncertainty Quantification for Multi-Modal LLMs
papers.abstract: Studies calibrated uncertainty quantification for multimodal LLMs, showing that uncertainty methods calibrated on text-only LLMs do not transfer well and proposing calibration that accounts for modality.
papers.oneLiner: Calibration tuned for text LLMs does not transfer to multimodal LLMs, so calibration must be modality-aware.
papers.keyFinding: Uncertainty calibration methods from text-only LLMs transfer poorly to multimodal LLMs, and modality-aware calibration improves reliability.
papers.weakness: Multimodal scope; relies on calibration/uncertainty proxies; limited model breadth.
papers.implication: Calibration must be tailored to the model/modality and its input distribution, which can vary across content types.
papers.contributions: Analysis of calibration transfer to multimodal LLMs; a modality-aware calibration approach.
papers.methods: Apply/tune uncertainty and calibration methods for multimodal LLMs; measure calibration error and selective-prediction quality.
papers.experiments: Multimodal LLM tasks; calibration and uncertainty-quality metrics vs text-only baselines.
papers.results: Text-only calibration transfers poorly; modality-aware calibration improves reliability.
papers.limitations: Multimodal-specific; not group-disaggregated; benchmark/scenario limited.
papers.futureDirections: Modality- and group-aware calibration; calibration for adaptive inference.
papers.insights: Calibration is input/modality-specific, so a single calibration may be unreliable for different input classes.
papers.relevance: Highlights that calibration (and thus early-exit confidence) is input-dependent, so different groups' inputs may be calibrated differently.

papers.title: The Well-Tempered Classifier: Some Elementary Properties of Temperature Scaling
papers.abstract: Study of the structural properties of temperature scaling, clarifying its role among calibration methods and its limitations, including conditions under which it is the only sensible post-hoc recalibration.
papers.oneLiner: Analyzes temperature scaling's structural properties and its role/limits among calibration methods.
papers.keyFinding: Temperature scaling is uniquely simple/robust among post-hoc calibrators, and its effectiveness is tied to assumptions about the label/score distribution that may not always hold.
papers.weakness: Theoretical treatment with limited empirical breadth; assumes a well-defined score/label distribution.
papers.implication: Temperature scaling is a convenient but assumption-laden calibrator; its single scalar cannot fix distribution- or group-specific miscalibration.
papers.contributions: Structural/theoretical analysis of temperature scaling; clarifications of when it is appropriate.
papers.methods: Theoretical analysis of temperature scaling properties; illustrative experiments.
papers.experiments: Classifiers/calibration datasets; ECE and reliability analysis.
papers.results: Temperature scaling is robust and often the only sensible global recalibration, but its single-parameter form limits group-specific correction.
papers.limitations: Theory-centric; does not address per-group calibration or adaptive inference.
papers.futureDirections: Group-conditional temperature; calibration under ambiguity; adaptive/selective calibration.
papers.insights: A single temperature cannot correct group-specific miscalibration — motivating per-group (or calibrated) exit thresholds.
papers.relevance: Reinforces that a single global temperature/exit threshold is insufficient for fair calibration across groups.

papers.title: Beyond Post-Hoc Temperature Scaling: Bilevel Optimization for LLM Calibration
papers.abstract: Proposes using bilevel optimization to calibrate LLMs, going beyond post-hoc temperature scaling by jointly optimizing the calibration with the model, improving calibration and robustness.
papers.oneLiner: Calibrates LLMs via bilevel optimization, going beyond simple post-hoc temperature scaling.
papers.keyFinding: Bilevel-optimized calibration outperforms post-hoc temperature scaling in calibration error and robustness, while integrating with preference-based training.
papers.weakness: Optimization cost/complexity; evaluation on calibration proxies; limited breadth of models/tasks.
papers.implication: Calibration can be integrated into training rather than applied post-hoc, enabling more precise (potentially group-aware) calibration.
papers.contributions: A bilevel-optimization calibration framework for LLMs; improved calibration and robustness over temperature scaling.
papers.methods: Bilevel optimization coupling model training with calibration; evaluated with calibration error.
papers.experiments: Multiple LLM tasks; calibration error and robustness vs temperature scaling baselines.
papers.results: Better calibration and robustness than post-hoc temperature scaling.
papers.limitations: Complex optimization; benchmark-dependent; not group-disaggregated.
papers.futureDirections: Group-aware bilevel calibration; calibration+fairness co-optimization; integration with early-exit training.
papers.insights: Calibration can be optimized end-to-end, opening the door to calibration-aware (and fair) exit policies.
papers.relevance: Suggests a path to train fairness- and calibration-aware early-exit heads rather than post-hoc adjusting thresholds.

papers.title: BERT Rediscovers the Classical NLP Pipeline
papers.abstract: Probes each layer of BERT with lightweight classifiers for syntactic and semantic tasks, showing representations encode information in a pipeline-like bottom-up order.
papers.oneLiner: BERT's layers recapitulate the classical NLP pipeline, with syntax emerging early and semantics later.
papers.keyFinding: Per-layer probing accuracy organizes into a clear bottom-up order (surface → syntactic → semantic), each task peaking at a characteristic depth and often declining afterward.
papers.weakness: Linear probes are read-only and show only what is decodable, not what the model uses; limited to BERT-base and English.
papers.implication: Representation 'maturity' is task- and depth-specific, so a fixed-depth readout (including an early exit) captures different information for different inputs.
papers.contributions: Layer-wise probing framework and a 'BERTology' map of where linguistic knowledge lives across depth.
papers.methods: Train linear/MLP probing classifiers on frozen per-layer BERT-base hidden states across 16 probing tasks; record accuracy per layer.
papers.experiments: 16 probing tasks (POS, constituents, dependencies, entities, semantic roles, coreference) on English corpora.
papers.results: Representational 'break points': POS peaks shallow, parsing mid, semantics near the top; accuracy often peaks then falls (non-monotonic deepening).
papers.limitations: Correlational probing on frozen features; English-only, task-limited; no causal use of representations.
papers.futureDirections: Causal knockout/ablation analyses; larger, multilingual, instruction-tuned models.
papers.insights: Maturity is not a single global property but a per-task, per-depth phenomenon.
papers.relevance: Supports the premise that layers reach probe-decodable ('mature') representations at different depths, the mechanism behind group-dependent early-exit gaps.

papers.title: The Bottom-up Evolution of Representations in the Transformer: A Study with Machine Translation and Language Modeling Objectives
papers.abstract: Studies how representations evolve layer by layer in Transformer MT/LM models, finding different types of linguistic information become separable at different depths and lower layers are more general while deeper are task-specific.
papers.oneLiner: Transformer representations specialize bottom-up, with each type of linguistic knowledge emerging at a distinct layer.
papers.keyFinding: Lower layers encode language-general features that transfer across objectives, while deeper layers encode task-specific information; specialization is incremental and bottom-up.
papers.weakness: Focused on MT/LM objectives; relies on correlational probing and layer transfer.
papers.implication: The 'maturity depth' of a representation depends on the information type, so shallow outputs retain general structure but miss deep task-specific signal.
papers.contributions: Systematic layer-wise probing and layer-transfer study across MT and LM models; evidence of bottom-up specialization.
papers.methods: Extract per-layer hidden states; probing classifiers plus layer transfer across MT and LM models.
papers.experiments: Transformer MT and language-modeling models; probing and layer-transfer analyses on standard MT/LM benchmarks.
papers.results: Layer-wise curves show syntactic vs semantic separation emerging at different depths; shallow layers transfer, deep layers do not.
papers.limitations: Narrow objective set; correlational probing; no demographic/subgroup analysis.
papers.futureDirections: Extend to classification, instruction-tuned and multi-attribute (demographic) probing across depth.
papers.insights: Specialization unfolds incrementally across depth, so shallow exits should miss deep task-specific signal.
papers.relevance: Core evidence that the content of representations — and hence their maturity — unfolds across depth, enabling depth-dependent group differences.

papers.title: Understanding Deep Neural Networks via Linear Separability of Hidden Layers
papers.abstract: Proposes understanding deep neural networks by measuring the linear separability of representations at each hidden layer, showing how separability grows with depth and relates to accuracy.
papers.oneLiner: Hidden representations become linearly separable as depth increases, yielding a quantitative 'maturity' measure per layer.
papers.keyFinding: Linear separability of hidden representations increases progressively with depth and correlates with task accuracy, offering a layer-wise maturity metric.
papers.weakness: Evaluated primarily on vision/feedforward architectures rather than Transformer LLMs; separability is dataset-specific.
papers.implication: Separability is a computable, quantitative proxy for representation maturity that can be measured per subpopulation.
papers.contributions: A layer-wise linear-separability measure as an interpretability/diagnostic tool.
papers.methods: Compute linear separability of representation at each hidden layer; relate to depth, accuracy, and model variants.
papers.experiments: Multiple deep networks and datasets; compare separability vs depth, accuracy, and network variants.
papers.results: Separability grows with depth and tracks higher task performance, peaking near the top.
papers.limitations: Not applied to LLM hidden states or demographic subgroups; architecture-centric.
papers.futureDirections: Apply to Transformer layers and compare separability across demographic groups.
papers.insights: Linear separability operationalizes 'maturity' and it is layer-dependent.
papers.relevance: Supplies the operationalization of 'maturity' (linear separability / probe accuracy) to compare across demographic groups at different depths.

papers.title: Investigating Gender Bias in BERT
papers.abstract: Measures how gender information is distributed across BERT's layers by probing each layer for gender and stereotypical associations, localizing where bias is strongest.
papers.oneLiner: Gender information is concentrated in particular BERT layers, and layer-wise probing localizes where stereotypes live.
papers.keyFinding: Gender bias is unevenly distributed across layers; a subset of layers is far more predictive of gender and stereotype associations, i.e., the bias 'matures' at specific depths.
papers.weakness: Encoder-only BERT, English, single demographic axis; probing is correlational and task-limited.
papers.implication: If gender is decodable mainly at specific layers, then the depth at which inference stops directly changes the amount of gender information available.
papers.contributions: Layer-wise gender probing and identification of the layers most responsible for gender/stereotype signals.
papers.methods: Probe each BERT layer with classifiers for gender prediction plus layer-wise WEAT-style association tests.
papers.experiments: BERT-base/large on gender prediction and stereotype-association tasks, layer-by-layer.
papers.results: Gender information is localized to a subset of layers and grows with depth, with middle-to-late layers most gender-predictive.
papers.limitations: Single attribute (gender), English, encoder-only, correlational probing.
papers.futureDirections: Larger decoders, other demographic axes, causal interventions.
papers.insights: A demographic attribute's representational maturity is layer-dependent — some layers 'specialize' in it.
papers.relevance: Core evidence that a demographic attribute's representation becomes separable (mature) only at certain depths, implying group-specific fairness effects at early-exit cutoffs.

papers.title: Locating and Mitigating Gender Bias in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Uses activation/influence analysis to locate which layers and modules in LLMs are responsible for gender bias, then mitigates it with targeted interventions.
papers.oneLiner: Gender bias is localized to specific layers and components, so it can be targeted rather than treated uniformly.
papers.keyFinding: Gender bias concentrates in particular layers and modules (often MLPs and attention at certain depths); removing it there reduces bias with minimal general-performance loss.
papers.weakness: Bias measurement is attribute/task-dependent; mitigation heuristics may not generalize across all bias types.
papers.implication: The depth at which outputs are taken changes the effective bias level, so early-exit depth selection is a fairness lever.
papers.contributions: Layer- and module-level localization of gender-bias components plus a targeted mitigation method.
papers.methods: Attribution/AIE-style analysis scoring each layer-module's contribution to gender bias; targeted intervention/debiasing.
papers.experiments: Several LLMs; layer-wise bias attribution and mitigation on gender-bias benchmarks and general task accuracy.
papers.results: Bias is concentrated in a small subset of layers; targeted intervention reduces bias with little accuracy loss.
papers.limitations: Gender focus; generalization to other axes untested; mitigation not fully principled.
papers.futureDirections: Apply to race and other attributes; combine with early-exit layer selection.
papers.insights: Certain layers are disproportionately responsible for demographic bias — the depth of inference changes measured bias.
papers.relevance: Directly ties layer depth to demographic-bias magnitude, the axis along which early-exit fairness gaps could emerge.

papers.title: Projective Methods for Mitigating Gender Bias in Pre-trained Language Models
papers.abstract: Examines how a gender subspace appears across the layers of pretrained LMs and compares projective methods that remove it, quantifying layer-wise bias strength.
papers.oneLiner: A gender subspace recurs across layers with varying strength, and projecting it out has layer-dependent effects.
papers.keyFinding: The feminine/masculine direction strength varies by layer (typically growing with depth), and projective debiasing behaves differently at different layers.
papers.weakness: Focus on the gender subspace in BERT-class encoder models; bias measured via a single-direction projection.
papers.implication: Since gender-direction strength is layer-dependent, exit depth directly affects how much gender information leaks into predictions.
papers.contributions: Layer-wise characterization of the gender subspace; comparison of projective debiasing methods across layers.
papers.methods: Compute gender directions per layer; evaluate PCA/hard/soft projective debiasing at each layer.
papers.experiments: Pretrained encoders (BERT/RoBERTa class); gender-subspace strength and bias metrics per layer under projective debiasing.
papers.results: Gender direction grows with depth; projective debiasing at deeper layers reduces bias more but can harm semantic content.
papers.limitations: English, gender-only, encoder models; projective debiasing has side effects.
papers.futureDirections: More attributes, decoder LLMs, interaction with depth-adaptive inference.
papers.insights: The strength of a demographic signal is layer-dependent, i.e., its 'maturity' varies with depth.
papers.relevance: Shows demographic (gender) signal strength is layer-dependent — matching the notion that groups' representations reach maturity at different depths.

papers.title: Gender Encoding Patterns in Pretrained Language Model Representations
papers.abstract: Probes how much gender information is encoded in pretrained LM representations and how this varies across layers and contexts.
papers.oneLiner: Gender information is encoded unevenly across layers and contexts, revealing where demographic signals live.
papers.keyFinding: The degree of gender encoding varies substantially across layers and depends on context, so no single layer is a uniform 'gender' source.
papers.weakness: Recent preprint with narrower gender scope and limited model coverage; probing-based (correlational).
papers.implication: Layer-dependent gender encoding means the information available at an early-exit depth differs across contexts and groups.
papers.contributions: Maps gender-encoding strength across layers and contexts in pretrained LMs.
papers.methods: Layer-wise probing of gender with linear classifiers on hidden states under varied contexts.
papers.experiments: Pretrained LMs; gender-probe accuracy per layer under different context conditions.
papers.results: Gender-probe accuracy varies by layer and context; some layers encode far more gender than others.
papers.limitations: Probing-based, gender-focused, no causal intervention or fairness metrics.
papers.futureDirections: Multi-attribute, causal analysis, integration with early-exit inference.
papers.insights: Demographic signal maturity depends on both layer and context, so different demographic inputs 'ripen' at different depths.
papers.relevance: Supports the premise that demographic-attribute representations mature at different depths, manifesting as group-dependent early-exit accuracy.

papers.title: Fine-Tuned Transformers Show Clusters of Similar Representations Across Layers
papers.abstract: Measures representational similarity (CKA-style) between all pairs of layers in fine-tuned BERT-like models, revealing that layers organize into clusters of similar representations.
papers.oneLiner: Transformer layers collapse into a few clusters of similar representations after fine-tuning, not a smooth gradient.
papers.keyFinding: Fine-tuned layers show block/clustered similarity structure (early, middle, late groups), so representation change is not monotonic and some layer groups are near-redundant.
papers.weakness: Focuses on representational similarity rather than task/attribute accuracy; encoder models only.
papers.implication: If layers form near-redundant clusters, exit-depth choice and per-group maturity differences depend on cluster boundaries.
papers.contributions: Quantitative layer-similarity (CKA) analysis of fine-tuned transformers revealing clustered structure.
papers.methods: Compute pairwise CKA similarity between layer representations of fine-tuned transformers.
papers.experiments: Fine-tuned BERT/RoBERTa variants on GLUE-style tasks; layer-by-layer similarity matrices.
papers.results: Similarity matrices show distinct clusters (lower/mid/upper blocks) with high within-cluster similarity and clear boundaries.
papers.limitations: Only fine-tuned encoders; no demographic attributes; similarity is not causal.
papers.futureDirections: Relate cluster boundaries to task/attribute 'maturity' and optimal early-exit depth.
papers.insights: Representations change in 'blocks' rather than uniformly, so maturity is lumpy — relevant to choosing exit depth and group differences.
papers.relevance: Characterizes how representations reorganize with depth, helping predict at which depth a group's information becomes (or stops being) separable.

papers.title: On the Effect of Dropping Layers of Pre-trained Transformer Models
papers.abstract: Investigates how much performance degrades when dropping individual (or groups of) layers from pretrained transformers, showing that not all layers contribute equally.
papers.oneLiner: Some transformer layers are nearly redundant or even harmful, so layer removal is surprisingly cheap.
papers.keyFinding: Many layers (including middle and some early ones) can be removed with minimal accuracy loss, revealing differential per-layer contribution.
papers.weakness: Layer removal is a crude proxy for early exit; not tested for subpopulation fairness; encoder-heavy.
papers.implication: Since layer importance varies, the depth at which inference stops does not preserve information equally across inputs.
papers.contributions: Systematic layer-removal/importance analysis across pretrained transformers.
papers.methods: Remove individual layers and layer groups; measure task-performance change; analyze layer redundancy.
papers.experiments: Multiple pretrained transformers across NLU/GLUE tasks; layer-dropping ablation.
papers.results: Performance largely retained after removing many layers, with a clear pattern of which layers matter.
papers.limitations: Removal (not adaptive exit) analysis; no demographic decomposition; limited task breadth.
papers.futureDirections: Study layer dropping by subpopulation; combine with adaptive early exit.
papers.insights: Layer importance is heterogeneous, so fixed-depth outputs are lossy per input.
papers.relevance: Establishes that information is distributed unevenly across layers, so the layer at which inference exits determines what (and whose) information is preserved.

papers.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Formally studies the linear representation hypothesis — that LLMs store features as directions in activation space — and analyzes the geometry of these representations.
papers.oneLiner: LLM features are stored as linear directions, giving a geometric basis for reading concepts from hidden states.
papers.keyFinding: Provides formal conditions and evidence that concepts are represented as approximately linear directions in activation space, supporting linear probing and steering.
papers.weakness: Theory-oriented with limited empirical breadth; no direct per-layer maturity or demographic subgroup analysis.
papers.implication: If concepts are linear directions, a linear probe at a layer measures how 'mature' a concept's direction is there.
papers.contributions: Formalization of the linear representation hypothesis; study of how features are inscribed as directions across the representation.
papers.methods: Theoretical representation/geometry analysis complemented by experiments probing linearity of concept directions in LLM activations.
papers.experiments: Probe/measure geometry of concept directions in LLM hidden states across models; tests of linearity and geometric structure.
papers.results: Many features are well-approximated by linear directions, with structure varying by layer and concept type.
papers.limitations: Limited empirical breadth; linearity is an approximation; not a fairness or per-layer maturity study.
papers.futureDirections: Extend to demographic directions and layer-wise maturity; connect to probing and steering.
papers.insights: Linear-probe accuracy at a layer is a principled proxy for the maturity of a (possibly demographic) concept's direction.
papers.relevance: Grounds the assumption that linear probing at a layer quantifies demographic-concept maturity, enabling depth-by-depth comparison of group representation maturity.
